This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for estimating eigenvalues in a high-dimensional Schrödinger equation. To address the lack of knowledge on proper regularization in this context, we focus on the eigenvalue-decomposition approach. By analyzing the relationship between the available data and the complexity of the problem, we establish a lower bound for the generalization error and demonstrate its applicability with numerical results. Furthermore, we determine the required data size for achieving a desired level of accuracy and examine the potential of utilizing less complex models to obtain comparable results. The findings are illustrated by numerical examples involving a high-dimensional square box, a multi-dimensional harmonic oscillator, and a multi-dimensional Rosenbluth system. The analysis demonstrates that the generalization performance can be improved by increasing the data size, utilizing a simpler model, or employing regularization techniques such as early stopping. The outcomes of this study are expected to expand to the estimation of other functional values. The source code for the numerical simulations is available at https://github.com/mathkakue/neural-networks-eigenvalue-problem. To the best of our knowledge, this the first time an in-depth generalization analysis has been conducted for the mentioned Schrödinger eigenvalue problems. The findings presented here provide theoretical support for the design of neural networks for these problems, which is in line with a growing trend in the field. This paper presents a short, uncomplicated proof that any Zinbiel algebra is in fact abelian. As part of the proof, it will be demonstrated that a derived algebra of a given Zinbiel algebra is also a homomorphically equivalent to the original algebra, establishing the basis for this claim. Additionally, it has been found that if a Zinbiel algebra is nilpotent to a certain order, its corresponding central derived series is similarly nilpotent to an order that is one step greater. It is further shown that under specific conditions, an extension of a nilpotent Zinbiel algebra is also nilpotent to a certain order within the extended algebra, while the associated extension of its commutator-derived algebra is nilpotent to an even greater order. These results yield the final finding that any Zinbiel algebra is abelian, which is demonstrated through an examination of a nilpotent algebra's largest abelian component and is further related to related results on nilpotent algebras. It is noted that the notion of abelian character within a Zinbiel algebra is equivalent to the notion of solvability. For a 3-dimensional focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation with zero-order inverse square potential and cubic interaction, we've established a new approach to examine the global Scattering in any initial condition possessing sufficient regularity. The key factor that enables this problem is the discovery of a specific conserved quantity, specifically the energy plus a new invariant, referred to as pre-scattering. The pre-scattering can be seen as a modified version of the standard Hamiltonian. By examining the behavior of the term operators in the linear equation corresponding to the pre-scattering, we've been able to bound its evolution over time. Utilizing these findings, we've proven that the pre-scattering is conserved numerically through the use of Galerkin approximations. Ultimately, we've been able to leverage these results to achieve the Scattering in 3d by constructing an outgoing solution from any given initial condition using the soliton-quantities identified by one of us previously. Those quantities include three solitons with radial symmetry as well as two solitons of rank one and two respectively, along with a linearly evolving term. The linearly evolving term can be obtained explicitly via Fourier transform and is solved for any initial condition. By examining the soliton-recombination of the three solitons, we've been able to Scattering-introduce a linearly evolving term for any bounded initial condition possessing sufficient regularity. While we've been able to obtain linear bounds for any initial condition possessing sufficient regularity using the term operators, we've been unable to locate any conserved quantity that includes the standard energy plus the term operators for any initial condition. Consequently, our findings suggest that the standard approach to locate linear bounds through the term operators may be insufficient to achieve the Scattering in this problem. A detailed numerical investigation has been conducted to verify our findings numerically through the use of Galerkin approximations. The numerical results have been replicated and confirmed by multiple code runs. Please note that our findings have been compared numerically with the findings obtained by Elganani in his recent study on the 1d focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation with inverse square potential. While our results appear to be consistent with the findings obtained by Elganani, we've been unable to locate any direct comparison between the two results. Consequently, our results should be interpreted as preliminary. Ultimately, our findings provide the first complete proof of the Scattering in 3d for any initial condition possessing sufficient regularity using the modified pre-scattering approach. We examine a complex model of interconnected populations, where each population represents a geographic zone, and analyze two key processes: a migration mechanism, which ensures that migrations between populations are mutually independent, and an infection mechanism, which simulates a viral transmission process, taking into account the global average infection rate and each population's specific infection rates. Taking a stochastic approach, our study focuses on the long-term evolution of this system, which allows us to draw conclusions about the system's future and interpret the results numerically. Furthermore, our investigation demonstrates that the system can reach a state where no new infections occur. Additionally, based on the system's initial conditions, our analysis shows that the system can either converge to an equilibrium or undergo permanent oscillations, and provides conditions for these outcomes as well as a detailed characterization of the system's future. In particular, our results show that the system tends to converge to specific values, which are either a single, zero, or infinite value, and the system's phase diagram is also explored numerically. Finally, our study demonstrates that the system can exhibit multiple, damped oscillations, which are characterized both analytically and numerically. The relevance of our findings to the COVID-19 pandemic is also discussed. The presented findings are originally from the author's PhD thesis. The system's orbital frequencies are linked by simple whole number ratios. By examining planetary mass distributions under different assumptions regarding their initial conditions, we investigated whether these planets could have evolved into their current orbits without mass loss from the parent star. The analysis showed that a power-law mass distribution could produce the required orbital frequency ratios, with approximately a 32% chance of success. Furthermore, our results suggest that a uniform mass array can form the Resonant Chain, with a probability of about 9%. However, when we applied random orbital phase initial conditions, our simulations yielded a much higher success rate of approximately 56%, indicating that these ratios are less challenging to achieve than initially thought. Using rectangular mass arrays as the basis for mass models, our models with a uniform mass distribution resulted in the Resonant Chain formation 98% of the time, whereas those without this constraint achieved the same outcome 100% of the time. Our calculations also showed that these orbital configurations can be maintained for a significant portion of the system's lifetime. The loss of material from the parent star through mass loss laws does not seem to be the primary driver of orbital period evolution in this system, with or without thermal evolution from the planets. With the constraint of maintaining the Resonant Chain configuration over a significant portion of its lifetime, our findings imply that the system should be observable through the orbital period gaps for at least half of its lifetime. Our models also match the observed changes in the orbital periods of the inner planets over time, with the outer planets displaying little to no change. The study utilized STM measurements to examine the Local Density of States (LDOS) of Graphite, Gold and Silicon surfaces. These measurements were conducted at varying temperatures, from 40K to 293K, utilizing a cryogenic STM setup. The experiment aimed to evaluate how lowering the sample temperature and utilizing STM imaging techniques, such as constant current mode, influence the STM images and the local samples' electrical conductivity. The results indicated that temperature has a significant effect on the STM measurements of the samples. The STM images of Graphite displayed more distinct molecular structures at lower temperatures, whereas the STM images of Gold and Silicon showed higher contrast between their individual constituent parts. The study provides valuable insights that can be employed to analyze and comprehend the STM images obtained during experimental studies. These measurements are particularly vital in various fields such as nanotechnology, research and development of new materials. The experimental results and their analysis are presented in the context of the course's educational objectives, demonstrating how these measurements can be employed to validate established theories on the behavior of electrons in solid substances and their impact on the samples' electrical conductivity. The discussion also highlights the significance of carefully selecting the experimental parameters to achieve the desired measurement results. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs remains the largest and most active repository of formal mathematics texts, having surpassed the 10-year milestone since its introduction. As Isabelle's leading contribution, Isabelle/IFP, designed for infinitary and functional logic, has been largely underutilized. Given the established tools and techniques, we aim to optimize Isabelle/IFP's performance by leveraging automation techniques such as interactively applying decision problem solutions for decidability. Furthermore, as a benchmark, we assess and refine the Archive's contributions of substructural or multi-modal logics by implementing and publishing a comprehensive, automated proof of the Craig's theorem, facilitating the integration of new languages within the Archive. Our results highlight the potential of careful, data-driven method application in enhancing understanding of a field, illustrating the importance of tools and techniques in theoretical analysis. We also provide a critical examination of common practices, offering means of further improving the efficiency and coherence of formal writing. By analyzing the performance of Isabelle/IFP's unexplored domain, we have developed a framework for critical assessment and strategic improvement of the Archive's contributions, with the ultimate goal of identifying and advancing the gaps in theoretical knowledge. As such, this study serves as an exemplar of how to implement and promote the use of theoretical results, employing the Isabelle toolset, within the scientific community. Furthermore, we have identified an array of open challenges for further investigation, potentially yielding new insights by adopting a similar approach in other areas for improvement within the Archive. A formal presentation based on this study is accessible at bit.ly/IFP-Thalhofer21. Besides the presented findings, we have also provided a list of suggested improvements for the Isabelle/IFP-related contributions in the Archive (available at bit.ly/IFP-Suggestions21). The accompanying material, including the implemented proofs, as well as further explanations and documentation, is provided at bit.ly/IFP-Supplement21. The provided source code can be accessed at bit.ly/IFP-Code-Main21 and bit.ly/IFP-Code-Support21. A foundational formal method is developed to analyze the behavior of GP2, a programming language designed for practical formal methods, which itself is built on a conservative extension of Hoare logic. A novel graphical syntax is introduced for GP2, complemented by a detailed operational semantics that breaks down the language's definitions into manageable Examines and Resolves operations. To capture complex library functions, GP2 allows for procedural combinations, which are central to its semantic definition, but pose a challenge due to infinite branching. A straightforward mini-step approach resolves this issue, making GP2's semantics unambiguous, while also enabling soundness and compositional proofs of its definitions. A detailed justification for this infinite branching scenario is provided, along with a demonstration of how GP2's semantics can be applied to examine Hoare logic's soundness. 

This work offers the first publicly available formal description of GP2's semantics, achieving a high degree of completeness and offering a range of beneficial consequences, including automatically verifying business logic, GP2 code, and interface contracts, as well as providing an operational re-implementation of the Verifying Classloader. Furthermore, a series of test cases with escalating difficulty have been used to validate the developed formalism, as well as its application to a novel formalisation of Java's object-oriented features. 

This work is based on the author's PhD thesis, with the most recent revisions having been made in July 2021. Relevant evidence, including a step-by-step guide to using the developed GP2 semantics and test case validation, has been made available online at: https://bit.ly/gp2-github.

The diversity of 2-20 mas radio structures observed in T Tauri stars remains to be fully explained by photoevaporation and MHD disk breeze models. Existing high-angular resolution observations are insufficient to conclusively validate either theory. We utilize the capabilities of the Large Millimeter Telescope/BISTI to conduct 1.3 cm band (23 mas) resolution studies of the TW Hydrae system, aiming to identify recurring radio morphological changes. After analyzing 22 observations over 11 years, we detected variable and stable morphological patterns, suggesting that the disk of TW Hydrae shifts between two dominant configurations. While the established MHD model can replicate the observed separation between the southern and northern components, it is unable to fully account for the size of the southern component during large-scale configurations. Furthermore, we estimate that the pionospheres corresponding to the large-scale configurations would need to be 0.1-1 au thicker than typically predicted by theories. We observe agreement between the MHD and photoevaporation theories for small-scale configurations (6-8 23 mas) and large mass loads (10^-8-10^-7 M[Sun, Zodier & Ag\"U 2018]), suggesting that the pionospheres in these instances are consistent with established thickness predictions (0.1-1 AU). We propose that the pionospheres in TW Hydrae may contain unmagnetized or weakly magnetized gas that fails to be effectively pumped by the MHD wind. As the first study to document extensive multi-year recurrence rates for TW Hydrae's radio morphology, our findings and analysis are expected to significantly contribute to the optimization of future observational campaigns, specifically those designed to distinguish between the predictions of photoevaporation and MHD models. Ultimately, our investigation into the TW Hydrae system serves as an optimal test case to evaluate the performance of photoevaporation and MHD models, paving the way for the investigation of similar systems, ultimately leading to a thorough understanding of the underlying physics. While the establishment of a comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics remains a pressing concern, our analysis indicates that the pionospheres in TW Hydrae could potentially be inextricably linked to the observed large-scale configurations (10-15 23 mas) of the system, possibly serving a key role in regulating the formation of the small pionospheres (6-8 23 mas) predicted by theories. In this context, we utilize machine learning to forecast beta-delayed neutron emission values, aiming to clarify the precision required for $r$process nuclear mass calculations. The precision required depends on the type of astrophysical event and the type of beta-delayed neutron emission. For example, we find that the precision required for the creation of elements during capture events is at a level of 0.1-0.2 nanobars, whereas precision up to 2 nanobars is needed for events resulting in neutron-poisoning processes. To support future $r$-process studies, we utilize machine learning to forecast beta-delayed neutron emission values based on known experimental data, aiming to incorporate these predictions into new mass tables. The machine learning model can also be applied to the prediction of mass values for nuclei that do not yet have experimental data, further supporting future $r$-process studies. Two-stage robust optimization problems with binary uncertainties are being increasingly used in various applications, but the main issue with current solutions is that they can only provide qualitative solutions due to limitations in expressing variable dependencies. In order to provide quantitative solutions, we propose a Lagrangian dual approach for these problems, formulated as a linearly constrained optimization problem with a variable objective function. However, due to the variable objective function, traditional convergence results are not available for this type of problem. Therefore, we first prove that under certain conditions, the Lagrangian dual has a continuous and differentiable graph, and then we provide a method for updating the Lagrangian dual solution. In order to overcome the issue of variable objective function, we propose a bisection approach to remove variables from the objective function one by one. We provide convergence analysis for this bisection approach and test it in various platforms, including machine learning, signal processing and data transfer, and the numerical results show that our solutions are very close to the lower bound of the optimal solution. Therefore, we can use our method as a lower bound optimizer to obtain better solutions for two-stage robust optimization problems. To tackle this issue, the concept of Socioeconomic Analytics within an Instance has been introduced, which enables instantaneous analysis and forecasting of SAE. A novel dataset, known as H4M, has been developed to facilitate the exploration and testing of SAE solutions through providing diverse datasets originating from multiple sources, viewed from multiple perspectives, and expressed in multiple forms. Currently, H4M comprises four datasets from the Beijing area, each containing four dimensions of observation, 94 quantitative fields, and 32 categorical fields. Additionally, these datasets have been expanded by combining data sources, removing data redundancy, and converting data formats, while also considering factors like data transmission, as well as accompanying metadata for further analysis. To the best of our knowledge, H4M is the first comprehensive dataset to facilitate research in the field of SAE. As such, it has been made publicly available at https://github.com/fanyu123/H4M. This research was a direct result of funding provided by the 2021 Beijing Economic Research Dataset Creation Program. We welcome researchers and practitioners to utilize H4M, provide feedback, and engage in collaborative research to advance the field of SAE. We look forward to seeing the diverse possibilities emerge from the H4M family, including H4M-KN-KN4M-KN4M-ZH. The research on Data Science has been accelerated due to significant advancements in the acquisition, storage, and analysis of vast, structured, and semi-structured digital contents. Recent breakthroughs have enabled the efficient processing of complex data at low costs, permitting analysts to focus on addressing the most complex problems. In this paper, we introduce the VisBigAll Ecosystem, a comprehensive framework for exploring and analyzing digital contents, and highlight the VisBigAll Ecosystem's support for the creation of customized data science pipelines and the exploration of large-scale digital collections. The VisBigAll Schema and its associated Digital Rearrangement Processes enable the adaptation and extension of the model to suit the needs of specific use cases, domains, and applications, contributing to a broader digital ontology and facilitating the evolution of digital contents over time. Deep neural networks are highly effective in handling input data with inherent structural properties, such as images and sound waves. Graph Neural Networks have gained traction in processing complex data patterns by modeling relationships within data. Despite advancements in GNNs, the field still lacks a comprehensive understanding of the underlying architecture of these networks. This research aims to bridge this knowledge gap in two ways. First, we have developed Gryph, a graphical toolkit that enables the creation of diverse graph neural network architectures by adjusting key design elements. This allows us to gain insights into the influence of these core components on a network's performance. Second, we have explored transfer learning within Graph Neural Networks, a computer science concept where pre-trained models are adapted for use in a variety of tasks. By establishing a performance trajectory for different GNN configurations based on varying task properties, we can forecast a model's performance before training. This research provides a deeper understanding of the graph neural network architecture, and holds promise for future optimization. The creation of Gryph allows for the flexible design of graph neural networks, and the examination of its components and their impact on a network's performance. This research brings transfer learning closer to real-world application by defining performance trajectories for graph neural networks based on task properties. The study finds that performance variability within a model is much more pronounced than across different models, and this variability heavily depends on task properties. These results suggest that there is still a lot to be gained from optimizing graph neural networks, and the development of more robust and reliable architectures is possible. In the service industry, customer satisfaction is crucial and can be significantly impacted by the quality of service received. Various forms of service quality, such as waiting time and problem resolution, are influenced by different factors. To improve service quality, a common approach involves providing additional resources to service channels when overloaded. Determining the optimal channel allocations, however, is a complex challenge. A proposed solution aims to mitigate this complexity by focusing on feature allocations as the primary objective. In this context, features represent specific service attributes such as "waiting time less than three minutes" or "problem resolved within 5 seconds". By controlling expectations on individual features, we can regulate overall service quality. A Dual Feature Allocation Model is developed to determine optimal feature-specific expectations and allocations, including the possibility of combining features to meet quality requirements. To address the complexity of this problem, an intelligent suggestion system is designed to provide viable solutions for real-world applications. In particular, this system is applied to the Amazon Mechanical Turk platform to yield effective suggestions and demonstrate feasible implementations. Additionally, a mathematical solution to this problem is explored through the formulation of a convex program, enabling the identification of optimal allocations when optimal service quality is defined. In cases where channel quality is a concern, an additional mathematical solution based on a Linear Programming reformulation is presented. The paper also delves into the relationship between the DFM and existing problems such as the multi-armed bandit problem and the linear programming relaxation of a cut packing problem, including the identification of optimal values for specific instances of these problems. Finally, theoretical bounds for the DFM solution are established using the obtained results. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed approach is throughly examined, showcasing its application and generalization potential to a variety of scenarios. In order to facilitate its use, a user-friendly open-source software implementation of the DFM solution has been developed, making it available for direct evaluation, as described in Section 7. A thorough analysis of the DFM solution quality is reported in the appendix. In particular, a relative gap between the DFM and LP solution is presented. A subsequent implementation of a DFM-LP solution that incorporates the theoretical bounds has also been developed, detailed in Section 8. A rational function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{P}^2$ is called bicritical if it induces mappings of degree $d$ in each affine chart and has precisely two fixed points within each chart. We explore the equivalent definition of a bicritical map being defined over the closure of its large-scale dynamical locus, known as its Fatou set. We describe a method for categorizing the geometric transformations of $f^q$ for a bicritical map $f$, and characterize the distinct types of iterative maps $f^q$ based on the structure of its invariant loci. We further discuss how the Fubiniyankov theorem can be applied to understand the topological properties of iterates $f^{k_1^{k_2}}$ of such bicritical maps. We note that bicritical maps are particularly abundant on certain specific models of hypersurface contact dynamics, such as right triangular motions. We conclude with several open questions and potential directions for future research. The Lord-Kohlmann-Arouhas time-resolved iteration technique expands upon existing methods for obtaining solution approximations to the Boltzmann equation, notably the spectral and Fourier-Fourier-Poisson methods. However, time-resolved iterations require dozens of parameter-dependent scaling combinations, resulting in computationally expensive simulations. To streamline this process, a new approach, time-resolved iteration with an inner iteration, demonstrates the potential for reducing the number of parameter-dependent scaling combinations to a manageable few. By proving its convergence to equilibrium in a rigorous mathematical framework, this enhanced iteration technique is shown to have the same underlying mechanism as the Fourier-Fourier-Poisson method. Moreover, when applied to a specific scenario with the linear Boltzmann equation, this improved iteration reduces the computational burden by a significant factor, yielding results much faster than the original time-resolved iteration. In particular, for a specific benchmark involving collisional gas flows with multiple scales, the inner iteration approach enables solutions to be obtained with significantly fewer parameter-dependent scaling combinations, resulting in substantial computational savings. The Horizon-10T collaboration reported numerous events in 2017 that, with high confidence, cannot be explained by background occurrences, which do not match any established source type. We propose that these unknown signals may be evidence of multiple quark nugget collisions resulting from the rapid freezing of the quark soup in an early universe scenario. Our analysis assumes that these quark nuggets caused the radiation of antimatter, grouping together at low energies as observed by Horizon-10T. Additionally, we will outline how these events could be further validated through the detection of additional signatures, such as electromagnetic emissions from the predicted remnants of a single quark nugget excited within a fermion-boson medium. If proven true, a detectable signature of the predicted fermion-boson medium is expected to be observed, which would provide clear evidence for quark nugget interactions. If the observed events are determined to be of a different nature, we provide alternative explanations based on the properties of isospin-invariant bosonic dark matter. Furthermore, we estimate the potential for detecting similar events resulting from the predicted collision of isospin-invariant color locks under similar analysis conditions. Last, we provide a possible explanation for the observed events, which aligns with the principles of quantum field theory. In 2021, the Axion Quark Nuggets collaboration reported a second group of events, which we propose can be completely explained by the predicted collision of isospin-invariant quark nuggets. Our analysis of this scenario assumes that these quark nuggets resulted in the emission of groupings of fermions and bosons, which partially excite the isospin-invariant quark nuggets, which are then partially excited before quickly decaying. Inspired by a desire to maintain confidentiality, we have developed a novel, lightweight form of steganography. By applying the principles of password protection to steganography, we have formulated the problem as a sequence-to-sequence task and proposed a neural network solution. This approach allows us to convert any input into a hidden message, providing near-perfect indistinguishability and undetectability as long as the sender and recipient share a known password. Additionally, our password-based steganography can handle both plain text and encrypted data, and its performance is enhanced by longer sequences and a stronger password. Furthermore, this method offers the following advantages over existing steganographic techniques: it produces text that is similar to natural language, its creation and detection processes are efficient, and it is resistant to attacks, particularly those based on Bayesian analysis. As a result, our sequence-to-sequence steganographic system is suitable for a range of confidentiality requirements. We have tested this method using multiple language models, a novel password-based encryption system, and the Long Short Term Memory algorithm. We have also collected and provided a dataset consisting of real-world conversations about a specific topic as part of the IR-8 championship, serving as a foundation for potential future research projects. We have performed an extensive analysis and provided multiple real-world examples of our solution. We have also compared our approach with relevant steganographic techniques and provided a detailed study and report on its performance. We are sharing our source code for others to use or reference at https://github.com academy/sequence-to-sequence-steganography. This research has the potential to contribute to the development of steganographic algorithms and the propagation of the field, leading to a potential future innovation and advancement in steganography and information security. We are confident that our solution represents an original and significant improvement in the area, and we are happy to share our work with others. While there are several forms of sequence-to-sequence steganography available, our solution is unique because it is the first to use a recurrent neural network to create steganographic text that is not only undetectable but also similar to natural language. This method enables simultaneous image capture and enables new possibilities of interactive imaging, and allows for the creation of a vast library of transient colors that can be activated at will between ordinary image states. We successfully demonstrate our system by creating never-before-seen colors and enabling never-before-seen effects of image transformation. Moreover, our system also allows for the extraction of filter properties which can be utilized for various applications such as material analysis, chemical detection, and more. By training a neural network to predict filter properties from images captured through a trained camera, we establish a new paradigm for computational imaging known as filter-forwarding, where the filter used to capture images can be inferred from images taken by another device with the same trained configuration. This information can then be utilized to activate dormant filter properties in the original image, and enables the creation of a vast library of transient filter properties that can be activated at will. This new paradigm enables a wide array of new imaging paradigms such as the discovery of unseen materials, and the creation of new effects of image transformation. We successfully demonstrate two new systems based on this paradigm: a system that enables a user to see the world through the eyes of a bee and a system that enables a user to discover invisible materials in the everyday environment. A Transit Feed Specification (TFS) compactly stores and presents parsed GTFS data in memory, enabling efficient processing and query operations. Nevertheless, working with TFS can be a complicated and technical task that demands substantial programming skills and knowledge of both TFS and the target application environment. As a result, we encounter significant obstacles in creating innovative TFS-based applications, leading to the federal government's data platform critique that TFS data is inaccessible. To mitigate this issue, we propose an open-source, user-friendly programming environment to create visualizations, reports, and other interactive products without requiring in-depth technical expertise. The core of our environment is an intuitive, visually-organized Python library that leverages a Recurrent Neural Torch model to generate customizable 2D representations of TFS data. By employing this environment, developers can produce high-quality, bus- and passenger-focused visualizations in a relatively straightforward manner, saving considerable time and resources. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our TFS-AI environment through real-world case studies of five distinct projects utilizing the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (LA Metro) TFS data. Woven into a narrative, we outline a step-by-step project pipeline to facilitate TFS data analysis and visualization. Specifically, we showcase three projects that employ data-driven and passenger-centric approaches: (1) Automatic generation of bus route maps (2) Personalized journey planning (3) Detection and analysis of hotspots. By leveraging the Recurrent Neural Torch model and our environment, we successfully overcome common programming challenges and successfully produce a wide-ranging, 3D visual representation of all 1.7 billion LA Metro stops, providing an in-depth analysis and better understanding of passenger behavior. As a result, we improve the quality of our passenger-focused 3D visualization by 30%, thereby paving the way for further optimization. Moreover, we anticipate that our environment will inspire other TFS data analysis and visualization initiatives, empowering a wider range of users to develop innovative applications. There is a pressing need to develop algorithms capable of tackling a wide range of data representation tasks, including dimension reduction, clustering, and more. A key challenge in this area is working with a minimal amount of sample data. Existing few-shot learning techniques primarily focus on metric-based algorithms, which require pre-trained bases to perform a projection. However, it's impractical and expensive to obtain a pre-trained base for every task, and it's also unclear how to effectively select these bases. Our main contribution is the introduction of a new paradigm for few-sample learning, which involves constructing multiple representative models for each category rather than relying on individual samples. Our method, which we call the 'Proto-Concentrate' framework, enables the generation of multiple prototype representatives for each category, achieving this by solving a regularized regression problem. Our category prototypes enable a range of tasks to be performed by processing data collections, including image clustering, image generation, and more. Our Proto-Concentrate framework allows the creation of state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods for both image and text domains, surpassing metric-based algorithms and establishing a new standard for few-sample learning. Future sky surveys, including the Rubin Surveyor formerly known as LSST, are projected to photograph a substantial fraction of the sky up to 200 times, resulting in a massive increase of around 10,000 times in the amount of data compared to the Dark Energy Survey. This vast data set encompasses diverse categories, including time-domain, structures, and quasars, which can be studied through various pipelines that all rely on a common step of classifying images. We examine the feasibility of employing Bayesian neural networks in the Rubin big data context, focusing on the effects of regularization and uncertainty estimation on the network's accuracy using a synthetic sky simulation, built upon the AstroDeep project. We find that adjusting the level of uncertainty in a Bayesian model can significantly impact its performance and is influenced by several factors, including the data quality and noise levels, while there appears to be an optimal level of uncertainty that yields superior results in terms of accuracy. We observe that not incorporating uncertainty when it is beneficial can reduce the model's effectiveness, and that an increased level of regularization beyond a certain point can damage the model's ability to accurately classify images. We find that precise astrometry and photometry are essential for the success of a Bayesian neural network, as these factors dominate the uncertainty in these parameters. This has significant implications for any pipeline that relies on these parameters as a key component, as this may involve a decrease of up to an order of magnitude compared to what has been previously proposed. We explore various ways to improve the precision of these factors while maintaining good image categorization accuracy, as this can be achieved through simple techniques that do not require substantial increases in computing power. Finally, we highlight the potential issues and improvements that could be implemented if the Rubin Surveyor were to repeat its observations of the same areas of the sky, as this could significantly reduce the amount of data under consideration, making it more feasible to match each image to a reference image from the survey. We further emphasize that utilizing the uncertainty associated with these classification tasks can greatly aid in reducing noise and improve our understanding of various cosmic phenomena, including gravitational waves, that rely on these classification tasks. This results in a nearly factor of two improvement in our ability to detect these waves and accurately measure key parameters such as the timing of the waves' arrival and their magnetic orientation. In general, we find that the uncertainty associated with these classification tasks can greatly aid the Rubin Surveyor's ability to achieve its stated goal of enhancing our understanding of the universe's late-time cosmology by at least an order of magnitude. Many combinatorial optimization problems are inspired by a new challenge called the Set-Union Knapsack Problem (SUKP). This problem is a combination of the well-known knapsack and set cover problems. A goal of the SUKP is to find a subset of items with the lowest total weight while covering at least a specified portion of a given set of items. The SUKP has close connections to other related problems such as the Budgeted Maximum Coverage issue. A key difference between these problems and traditional combinatorial optimization issues is that their optimal solutions may not have proportional costs. As a result, finding exact solutions using methods like linear programming can sometimes result in infeasible solutions due to fractional costs. The Budgeted Maximum Coverage issue extends the SUKP by allowing a limited budget for costs, with the goal of covering as much data as possible within that budget. A method for solving both the SUKP and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage issue is called Multi-productive Multi-budgeted Multi-covering (MMMC). The key component of the MMMC algorithm is a modified search technique that continually evaluates and selects the best nodes in the search tree based on the goodness of their partial solutions. The MMMC algorithm is capable of producing both a partial covering and a partial costing solution. The performance of the MMMC algorithm was evaluated using 60 publicly available SUKP instances and the results showed that it outperformed other widely used search techniques. The MMMC algorithm was further improved by incorporating a mechanism to limit the depth of the search tree. The resulting version of the MMMC algorithm is called MMMC' and it outperformed all other search techniques when evaluated using 60 partial SUKP instances with very large sizes. The MMMC algorithm and its variant MMMC' were successfully used to solve a real-world application involving the SUKP. The solution using MMMC' was certified as the optimal solution and it was successfully implemented in a real-world setting. The results of the experiment showed that MMMC' consistently found the optimal solution and it was the only search technique that could prove its results. The time taken by MMMC' to solve the optimal solution varied greatly depending on the size of the instance. The variant of the MMMC algorithm that used a mechanism to limit the depth of the search tree performed significantly better than the other search techniques when evaluated on very large partial SUKP instances with very large sizes. To assess the risks that cyclists face, we need to measure not only the probability of accidents, but also their potential severity as well. In order to evaluate relative risk levels, a predictive model must be able to account for how the probability and severity of accidents change in response to varying cycling conditions. In the absence of relevant data, a framework must be utilized to estimate accident probabilities through statistical analysis. This research introduces a novel scoring method that calculates total risk by combining probability and severity of accidents, accounting for the fact that cyclists are more likely to avoid low-severity accidents. In order to determine total risk, the research considers the impact of bicycle design flaws on the frequency of accidents and accounts for the fact that advanced riders are less likely to experience accidents in the first place. This research utilizes a large video dataset of cyclists and applies deep learning to estimate total risk levels. In order to quantify the impact of bicycle design features on accident probabilities, the research utilizes expert feedback and applies utility calibration to ensure that the predicted probabilities reflect the opinions of average cyclists. The research finds that the total risk levels estimated by our model correlate strongly with existing safety ratings of bicycles. In addition, the research conducts a comprehensive analysis of how total risk levels change in response to varying bicycle design features and riding conditions. This research has significant practical applications, as it can be utilized to create an interactive safety assessment tool that helps cyclists and bicycle manufacturers identify and prioritize the most critical safety risks. To accelerate the learning process of model-free reinforcement learning agents, experience replay is highly effective. The standard approach of replaying experiences at random intervals can be inefficient, as it may not leverage the information contained in recent experiences. Recent studies have demonstrated that prioritized experience replay, which assigns higher priorities to experiences with larger rewards and updates more frequently, can accelerate learning. However, this method is often plagued by divergence issues, as updates to similar experiences can push them further away from their optimal targets. We have developed a new variational approach to experience replay, which assigns experiences to batches based on their proximity and updates them by minimizing the distance between them and their corresponding target distributions. This is achieved through a variational quadratic loss function, which is efficiently optimized using the conjugate gradient method. Our proposed algorithm, variance decrease, achieves convergence to optimal policy performance, as the target distribution varies, under certain conditions. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that variance decrease is a scalable and efficient method for experience replay. When compared to other reinforced learning baseline methods, it consistently achieves stable convergence and rapid learning across multiple environments, particularly in complex high-dimensional settings. Moreover, we have found that variance decrease can be used as a post-post optimization technique, as it can further improve model performance beyond that obtained through post optimization. Specifically, our proposed model, PPO-E, which combines PPO with variance decrease, is able to robustly generalize to multiple settings, as it reduces the impact of optimization by minimizing the variance of the policy gradient. Furthermore, variance decrease can be adapted for use in conjunction with other reinforced learning baseline methods, including Q-learning, as it can enhance its stability and robustness by reducing divergence. Our results also highlight the advantages of variance decrease when applied to learning in partially observable Markov decision processes. Overall, variance decrease represents a novel and efficient approach to experience replay, which can be used to accelerate learning and improve model generalizability across multiple settings. Future work may involve extending this method to accommodate changing reward functions, as well as its application in multiple settings. Our research demonstrates that, by leveraging multi-language programming, we can concurrently manage memory safety and performance considerations. Specifically, Josephine achieves a 5.8x speedup over an all-Rust implementation, with an average gain in performance of 2.7x when running on Node.js with Josephine compared to its native Node.js counterpart for various benchmarks. Moreover, Josephine's runtime integration of Rust and JavaScript enables the creation of memory-safe, standalone JavaScript programs, accompanied by a newly introduced benchmark suite titled 'jester.' Finally, our approach provides a general framework for allocating and managing memory in languages providing a runtime interface, complemented by a discussion of potential future research avenues inspired by this work. This research explores a novel process where a nucleus undergoes transform into three particles upon interaction with a high-energy electron. We investigate the connection between this rare event, primarily a sign of Majorana particle nature at a large distance, and a rare event detected at the Large Hadron Collider. We have discovered a transition period, stretching from the moment an electron interacts with the nucleus to the instant the triad of particles is formed, in which the amplitudes of the two types of transitions, collectively called 'neutrinoless', start out with significant differences only to later converge as the distance between the electron and the triad increases. As the mass of the electron increases, the likelihood of the event, referred to as 0νEE', grows and eventually exceeds the likelihood of the event, referred to as 0νμμ'. We demonstrate that if the mass of the electron exceeds the combined mass of the triad by a factor of 10, the event, referred to as 0νEE', will far exceed the likelihood of the event, referred to as 0νμμ'. Importantly, the event, referred to as 0νEE', occurs much faster than the event, referred to as 0νμμ', and this property, combined with the fact that the triad is created far from the nucleus, makes it feasible to detect this type of rare event through observation of the triad formed at a detector located far from the nucleus, using the Large Hadron Collider as a type of beta-doublet factory. We have proposed a number of experiments aimed at detecting this rare event, including the study of electron upgrades, particle nucleus combinations, particle collisions with the nucleus, and the experiment involving the nucleus under the influence of a strong magnetic field. Recent advancements in belief propagation list decoding have focused on enhancing the decoding performance and efficiency of polar codes by using multiple iterative algorithms in parallel. Building on previous work that combined the polar subcode and sub-division list decoders, this paper takes a step further by incorporating multiple iterative algorithms into the subcode method. Similar to the sub-division list decoder, the proposed approach is based on the subcode principle, with an added benefit of increased flexibility that allows for seamless adaptation of various list decoder configurations. Furthermore, the paper provides a systematic framework for analyzing and comparing different parallelized settings. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly improve the decoding performance, with some variants surpassing the subdivision list decoder in both error rate and subcode depth. Moreover, the paper investigates the decoding latency, with findings suggesting that the trade-off between decoding performance and latency is heavily dependent on the specific parallelized algorithms used. As a result, the choice of algorithms becomes a crucial factor in determining the overall benefits of parallelization. Experimental data indicate that the second-order Newton Iterative algorithm, when applied extensively, may not provide significant improvements over its single-iterative counterpart, whereas other algorithms like the second-order iterative algorithm show more promising results, with potential gains up to several kilometers when used in parallel. In summary, the proposed approach offers enhanced flexibility in list decoders by allowing for multiple iterative algorithms to be easily integrated into the subcode method, with the choice of algorithms playing a crucial role in optimizing decoding performance and latency. Experimental results with various code lengths and code rates have been presented, with the source code for the decoders being openly available on the repository: https://github.com/alištos/bpld. Additionally, the decoders have been successfully implemented as soft- and hard-bit decoders in the IEEE 802.11be standard. Furthermore, the paper's findings contribute to the understanding of the general principles underlying the subcode method in belief propagation list decoders, with the subdivision list decoder being reinterpreted as an iterative algorithm of order one, resulting in the proposed framework as an iterative algorithm of order two or higher, with the subcode method being parallelized using multiple iterative algorithms of various orders, with the choice of algorithms again depending on the desired trade-off between decoding performance and latency. This threshold depends solely on the size of the computational domain and the vorticity's supremum for the given conditions at an infinitesimally small timeframe. It's essential to note that $\beta^2_s$ can be viewed as an indicator of the vorticity's integral growth over time. If the vorticity's supremum remains finite for all time, the threshold will be zero, indicating that the vorticity can be resolved without restriction. This theory also enables the estimation of the minimum necessary resolution to prevent numerical instability when the vorticity's behavior is unpredictable. This approach is exemplified through practical experiments, including the simulation of the Taylor-Gouye column and the non-critical Taylor-Couette flow, both featuring finite vorticity growth over time. Furthermore, we propose that the vorticity's growth can be effectively modeled using a particular differential equation, allowing the calculation of an optimal, finite resolution requirement for both finite-time and infinite-time scenarios. This resolution requirement is influenced by the vorticity's characteristic frequency, its size, and the Reynolds number. This structure enables straightforward generalization to various flow geometries, and the corresponding factors can be determined through linear stability analysis. Cells are the basic building units of life and have been the subject of fascination for scientists and the general public for centuries. Recently, there's been a growing interest in the 'creativity in biology' field, which involves using artificial intelligence to generate cell representations and simulate cell development. Most existing cell models are based on explicit parameterization, but this approach can be limited by its reliance on manually defined parameters. In contrast, implicit neural representations offer greater flexibility and potential for more accurate representations. However, existing implicit models require large amounts of high-quality data, which can be challenging to obtain in the biological field. To address this challenge, we introduce a new technique that allows us to generate synthetic data during the training process, enabling the use of implicit neural representations even with limited data. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in generating cell representations for two applications: modeling cell shapes and simulating cell development. Our results suggest that synthetic data augmentation can be a valuable tool for developing accurate and flexible cell models, even with limited data. We also note that existing tools lack sufficient high-quality cell data, so a significant opportunity exists for the biological community to contribute. Our hope is that others in the biological modeling community can benefit from these findings. The code for our research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/krishnanukil/BotCell-Auto.

As image-based PDFs become increasingly prevalent, the accessibility of digital documents for the benefit of readers with impairments is severely compromised. I argue that the primary culprit behind this problem is the prevalent use of image-based PDFs, specifically those generated by printers, scanners, and online tools such as Google Docs. These types of PDFs are not only commonly employed but are also often the only feasible option for creators, rendering conventional reading methods inaccessible to impaired readers. To address this, readers must rely on more laborious and error-prone methods, such as manual text transcription, to access content, a process that is both time-consuming and arduous. To highlight the necessity of document accessibility, I share two personal accounts from my own experiences, one being the need to access a medical report and understanding a new medical condition, and the other involving accessing document needed for legal proceedings. Ultimately, the need for document accessibility has sparked a necessary movement, with individuals and organizations working to create awareness and promote accessibility among document creators, with far-reaching and beneficial consequences. Understanding the magnitude of this problem and the severity it causes to impaired readers is crucial in fostering a collective effort to create a culture of accessibility and to advocate for document accessibility laws and technologies that protect and empower readers with impairments. To achieve this goal, a new kind of PDF— the Accessible PDF—is introduced, one that preserves the graphical integrity of a document while making its text searchable and readable. Through the development of a web-based converter, readers with impairments can easily obtain Accessible PDFs from their corresponding image-based PDFs. By making existing document creators produce more accessible outputs, a new kind of PDF— the Accessible PDF— is created, aiming to improve document accessibility and empower readers with impairments to access their needed information in a more efficient and smooth way. Ultimately, a note on how to make image-based PDFs accessible through existing document evaluation technologies, including PDF accessibility evaluators and text-to-speech readers, is presented. Notably, the majority of these tools are found to be ineffective in addressing the document accessibility challenge, underscoring a pressing need for creators to invest in document accessibility. To mitigate this issue, the importance of educating document creators on the importance of document accessibility is emphasized, as well as the need to establish a culture of accessibility among PDF creators. To overcome these limitations, the need for innovative document accessibility technologies and document accessibility laws and regulations is proposed, with a long-term goal of perfecting the existing document accessibility technologies that already evaluate image-based PDFs.

We present XL-net, a pre-trained language model that excels in various
downstream tasks and matches or surpasses the state-of-the-art performance of BERT and RoBERTa models. XL-net incorporates an autoregressive pre-training method like BERT, but in a more efficient manner by using anarchy transformers in its pre-training stage. This approach allows the model to capture both forward and backward contextual information at the same pre-training level, resulting in significant performance improvements. Our extensive testing reveals that XL-net outperforms BERT and RoBERTa models in multiple downstream tasks, achieving an average increase of 0.65% on the GLUE benchmark. Additionally, XL-net showcases superior scalability by achieving faster training and inference speeds than BERT and RoBERTa models. Our research demonstrates that XL-net's advantages in various downstream tasks are largely due to its pre-trained model performance, not its tokenization strategy. Our results also highlight the models' strengths and weaknesses by analyzing their saliency maps and feature representations. The search for exoplanets with atmospheres that are capable of supporting life depends heavily on the technique of analyzing transit spectroscopy, which is vulnerable to the interference caused by stellar activity. We explored how different analysis methods, specifically removing signals with low or high resolution, impact the detection of Planetary Systems. We utilized computer simulations to analyze the effects of various low-resolution phenomena on mock low-resolution spectra, measuring the strength of the Halpha line as a result. The analysis showed that incorporating radial velocity variations, which reflect the star's surface activity, significantly improved our understanding of the activity's impact, surpassing the effects of photometric variability. We found that high-resolution spectroscopy is essential for accurately detecting Earth-like planets and is particularly crucial for systems similar to the Sun, which is likely due to the differences in the characteristics of active regions and starspots. We observed that in systems similar to the Sun, using high-resolution spectroscopy yields more reliable results, while also revealing the potential for accurately detecting the biosignatures in atmospheres of habitable-Zones exoplanets, such as those orbiting KOI-3123 and the TRAPPIST-1 system. However, in systems with extremely active sun-like stars, even high-resolution spectroscopy may not be enough to accurately detect the presence of terrestrial exoplanets, which could explain the failure of various space missions to detect such planets. We suggest that incorporating simulated analysis methods, specifically removing signals with low or high resolution, and considering radial velocity variations, photometric variability, and planetary radius is essential for accurately detecting the presence of terrestrial exoplanets, which could potentially utilize the Kepler mission's data. The algorithm was applied to various planets in the Kepler 111701 and TRAPPIST-116 systems to confirm the effectiveness of incorporating simulated analysis methods in the search for exoplanets with habitable-zone super-Earth atmospheres, such as those in the TRAPPIST-116 system. Several differentiation-based methods have effectively addressed the challenging dispersive behavior present in tsunami wave propagation, particularly in scenarios such as tsunami events triggered by asteroid collisions. Although specialized finite element methods like the Generalized Finite Element Method have shown potential in tackling the tsunami's high-frequency waves, efficient modeling of the low-frequency, strongly dispersive waves often requires a more refined approach. This study contributes an improved, time-domain differentiation-based method for strongly dispersive wave modeling with the strong-form Galerkin approach, where a standard linear element with adapted interpolators is used. This method overcomes limitations of the existing path-dependent strong-form methods, allowing for unrestricted spatial flexibility and more efficient modeling of the tsunami's initial stages. A crucial step in the Heuristics for Flexible Manufacturing Systems (H-FMS) framework is scheduling, which incorporates uncertainty into two main categories: time-based and date-based variability. Despite the significance of date-based uncertainty to real-world manufacturing scenarios, current H-FMS approaches primarily focus on time-based uncertainty. This paper addresses this limitation by outlining a comprehensive method for incorporating date-based uncertainty into system parameters, processing time, and resource availability. A case study was conducted to evaluate the performance of this approach in comparison to a model assuming all processing times are fixed and to a model using stochastic sampling for variable times. Results indicate that both uncertain models outperformed the deterministic model in real-time performance; however, the model incorporating a diverse set of variable times surpassed the model using variance-based variables. This new approach enhances the realism of date-based uncertainty in manufacturing management, allowing for more accurate system modeling and scheduling in the context of the H-FMS framework. Recent advancements in word embedding have significantly enhanced software application potential for real-world purposes. However, numerous software development platforms continue to face issues related to data written in non-standard language forms, such as social media platforms receiving code-mixed input in multiple languages. Despite the growing importance of processing such code-mixed data, very few models have been specifically designed for this task. Existing models have attempted to address this, but either rely heavily on pre-existing word embeddings or employ intricate syntactic analysis with high computational costs. In response to this, we have developed the Transition Point-based Dynamic and Relative Positional Encoding (PEOTO) model, which encodes word meanings dynamically based on transition patterns and leverages positional information in a neural network framework. Thoroughly evaluated on multiple code-mixed language datasets, our model has achieved superior performance compared to existing models. Moreover, we have observed that the Peoto- Hajmola model, which employs a small, compact architecture, exhibits outstanding robustness in face-to-face multilingual conversation scenarios despite varying input orders. The potential of this model to efficiently process code-mixed input makes it highly suitable for social media monitoring applications in multiple languages. Although iron-based superconductors exhibit various anisotropic responses, a specific response related to nematic order remains absent in the studied compound, LiFeAs. This lack raises questions about the origin of static and dynamic nematic instabilities observed in other iron-based superconductors. To address this, we examined LiFeAs's magnetic structure using neutron scattering and found that its local moment arrangement and magnetic fluctuations are significantly reduced compared to other iron-based compounds. Furthermore, small-wavelength oxygen-peak fluctuations are nonexistent, and the associated wavevector is not a point of magnetic instability. To enhance the effectiveness of BERT models in specific tasks, the technique of task-adaptive pre-training has been explored. This method involves adding a small task-specific layer to the BERT model, training it with task data, and thereby enables the BERT model to utilize richer information for task inference. However, a major drawback of this technique is that the large-scale pre-trained BERT model and the task-specific layer may not have a clear boundary, making it difficult to decouple their respective contributions to the final result. Furthermore, the task-specific layer's capacity is generally limited, which can result in information loss occurring when task information is embedded to the pre-trained BERT model. A novel method called Dict-BERT is proposed in this research to address the above issues. The core idea of Dict-BERT lies in dynamically expanding the task-specific layer's capacity through a parallel training process with a small attention mechanism and a dictionary that maps task words to word embeddings via a word map. Consequently, the task-specific dictionary of Dict-BERT makes it possible to achieve a clear boundary between the task-adaptive BERT model and the pre-trained BERT model, thus allowing the large-scale pre-trained BERT model to fully leverage its advantages in pre-trained capacity. Experimental results show that Dict-BERT outperforms other models, including the original BERT and various task-adaptive pre-training methods, on eight specific NLP tasks. Federated learning is a distributed machine learning technique that enables secure collaboration on sensitive data without exchanging actual records. This is achieved by having a central server guide and consolidate models while participating clients contribute local data and model updates. A key challenge in FL is mitigating pragmatic attacks by manipulating model updates to compromise client privacy, which can be particularly harmful in regulated industries. Despite existing research primarily focusing on horizontal FL, recent findings indicate that similar attacks can also succeed in vertical FL, where attackers aim to combine datasets from multiple parties, by gaining access to several models after each learning cycle. Our work builds upon this discovery by proposing the first formal definition of privacy breaches in vertical FL and an associated attack detection method using Bayesian networks. This method was evaluated on several scenarios where it consistently outperformed existing approaches in detecting privacy breaches in vertical FL. Notably, it was found that vertical FL environments are more susceptible to pragmatic attacks compared to horizontal FL environments, with a significant 5-8 times higher success rate. This difference highlights the importance of adapting and enhancing privacy enhancement techniques to accommodate the unique characteristics of vertical FL. Additionally, our research reveals that vertical FL environments are often required to adhere to stricter privacy and regulatory requirements, such as HIPAA, due to the sensitive nature of involved datasets, which is a key differentiator compared to horizontal FL. Overall, our research aims to fill the knowledge gap in pragmatic attacks on vertical FL and pave the way for future investigations. This research is expected to be particularly valuable for regulatory bodies, as it has been estimated that regulating 10-20 industries would generate around $2.5 trillion in economic benefits, primarily due to the primary sector of Commerce but also impacting other sectors like Healthcare. By extending existing research from horizontal to vertical FL, our work can help determine the most effective techniques to regulate and mitigate pragmatic attacks. Using the Healthcare sector as an example, our research indicates that if the US government spends around $3 billion annually to regulate technology providers, it could lead to the generation of around $2.5 trillion in economic benefits, which surpasses the costs of regulating commerce by around $2 trillion. This is because the Healthcare sector is a key area where federated learning is expected to make a significant difference in improving data quality and patient outcomes, which is likely to be compounded by the growing popularity of FL in this field. Therefore, our research has the potential to contribute to the US economy by around 0.1-0.2% by paving the way for the adoption of FL in the Healthcare and Commerce sectors.

A traditional method for document retrieval involves assigning a weight to each document based on its relevance to a given query, with more relevant documents receiving higher weights. However, when a large dataset is truncated for training purposes, as is often the case with label noise ranking, the assigned weights may not accurately reflect the original relevance, leading to suboptimal retrieval performance. To mitigate this limitation, we developed a training sampling algorithm that mimics the original dataset's structure and distribution, allowing for accurate retrieval even when the training dataset is significantly smaller than the full dataset. Furthermore, we addressed the issue of adaptive sampling by developing a cluster-wise loss function that enables learning to prevent overfitting. The proposed method was successfully tested on two real-world datasets and was shown to surpass the performance of traditional methods with truncated training data. Specifically, our approach demonstrated notable improvements, with retrieval accuracy exceeding that of traditional methods by 15% and 10% on the CDIR and WIKIGAN datasets, respectively. Despite GNNs' exceptional performance with sufficient labeled data, most studies have highlighted the significant limitations they face when working with limited or partially supervised data. We test the efficacy of this approach on six diverse graph data sets, observing significant improvements in terms of performance. The findings suggest that this approach consistently outperforms established methods, delivering robust results even in extremely adverse conditions. This research examines how differences in the plasma's radial dimensions and off-center electron injection affect the resulting beam dynamics and betatron radiation spectra emitted by witness electron particles in proton-driven plasmas. We develop a customized method to efficiently calculate the R\'enyi divergence between two probability distributions. Although the R\'enyi divergence is not always differentiable, we create a smooth variant by adding a Cauchy regularizer, resulting in a differentiable function. Building upon this, we design a closed-form optimization technique to find the argument that minimizes this new, smooth R\'enyi divergence. In addition, we extend this method to accommodate multiple such divergences and apply it to various applications, including feature selection and classification, where it achieves comparable results to existing techniques based on the Kullback-Leibler divergence but with the benefit of faster computation times. Moreover, we investigate the conditions under which our method is guaranteed to work effectively in theoretical terms. Our approach is made available as the rdivreg R-package, which allows for easy and flexible use of our method in a variety of settings. We illustrate its utility with several examples, demonstrating its ability to handle various probability distributions and data types. This work presents a detailed examination of the outcomes generated by an anisotropic curvature-flattening algorithm, which flattens polygons in a manner similar to a specific variant of mean curvature flow in geometry. The proposed idea is to investigate the dynamics of a polynomial's average curvature, treating it as a variable factor in a system of equations that describe the shape's movement. The study is organized into two primary sections, with the first exploring the behavior produced by an isotropic curvature-flattening algorithm, which shows how the initial polygon's boundaries change into a sequence of curves. These curves are arranged in a way that their sums equal the graph of a single function. The second part delves into the anisotropic case, where the algorithm takes into account an average curvature that varies based on a parameter. In this instance, the algorithm produces a sequence of polygons whose edges form the basis of a specific class of partitioned regions. The study demonstrates how the type of surface generated by an isotropic algorithm resembles those obtained from Baire category theory's categorial components. Similarly, the anisotropic case produces partitions that are akin to stable manifolds within the Mandelbrot set family. The last section discusses potential extensions to these concepts in higher-dimensional scenarios and the related projections, as well as the broader implications and connections to other surface-related theories, particularly in the context of Euclidean geometry. The study also acknowledges and integrates relevant prior works in the field. The related proofs are included in the appendix for reference. Our novel approach for training deep learning models involves utilizing a specialized discipline: hortography, the study of plant morphology. By generating realistic yet controlled environments for analyzing plant shapes, we create an immersive world called GrowSpace where virtual plants can be raised and examined from different perspectives. Through this immersive world, we demonstrate a model called MoldNet that learns to predict the shape of plants under various external influences such as packing, stretching, bending, and adjustments in growth duration and rate. MoldNet not only outperforms baseline models but also exhibits enhanced versatility by enabling the generation of synthetic data and the creation of realistic plant representations. Additionally, we develop HORTO, a comprehensive library for generating artificial plant images, and introduce multiple challenges to push the boundaries of training deep learning models in GrowSpace. By showcasing the effectiveness of our approach, we highlight its potential applications in various disciplines including computer vision and plant biology. The source code for our model and associated utilities can be accessed at https://mold.net.ua.de/

We introduce a groundbreaking training method for deep learning models that mimics expert-controlled experiments.
We create an innovative GrowSpace environment for modeling plant development in various external environments and predicting optimal shapes.
Our MoldNet model leads the field in predicting plant shapes under multiple external influences.
Our model enables the creation of synthetic data and realistic plant representations.
We develop an end-to-end solution, incorporating a GrowSpace environment, MoldNet model, and HAUT library for generating artificial plant images. We propose an explanation for the generation of primordial black holes within our universe. Our model relies on the theory of curvaton, where a hypothetical field called the curvaton is believed to cause cosmic inflation. However, in our version of the theory, the curvaton is described by a modified equation known as the Palatini action, leading to what some might consider an unconventional, unpalatable universe. Despite this, we've found that the curvature perturbations produced by this field are compatible with observational standards. Furthermore, when we applied the theory of gravitational instability to the conditions of the Palatini curvaton universe, we discovered that the curvature perturbations are large enough to create primordial black holes in some areas. Our estimates suggest that the abundance and mass of these black holes vary depending on the potential parameters of the curvaton. Specifically, we've found that our version of the theory could potentially account for the generation of dark matter and the observed anomalies in the universe's monolithic disks, all within the framework of the Palatini formalism. If our findings are correct, it would indicate that the universe's density fluctuations arise from quantum fluctuations during a phase known as the starobinsky inflation, rather than relying on the simpler, better-known scalar inflation theory. While our version of the theory is complex and requires further validation, it does provide an original and innovative explanation for the generation of primordial black holes. If the predictions of our model are observed in future experiments, it would provide strong evidence for the success of the Palatini formalism in cosmology. In particular, we've suggested that experiments like the Square kilometer Array should be able to detect gravitational waves from the inflationary era in the very near future. If these waves are not detected in the near future or if they are not found to match the predicted patterns, it would indicate a significant discrepancy between our theoretical model and the reality of the universe. In particular, it would raise questions about the success of the Palatini formalism in describing gravity and cosmology. In the worst case, it would indicate a significant problem with our understanding of the universe and the validity of the theoretical model of the Palatini formalism as a description of cosmology. One of the potential issues that could arise if the predictions of our model are observed in future experiments and the reality of the universe does not match the predicted patterns is that our understanding of the generation of density fluctuations during inflation and the universe as a whole could be significantly revised.
