We examine how grammatical gender influences word representations in languages that indicate gender and find that the effect of gender is a significant factor in determining the similarity between related species names and the parent genus name. We discover that the predictability of gender within a language correlates with smaller differences in vector distance between associated names, and that the European languages' higher predictability rate results in smaller differences compared to non-European languages. We develop a new, simple method to predict and evaluate the ease of grammatical gender indication, which reaches 57.1% accuracy without any linguistic expertise in high-predictability languages of English. We further explore the impact of education on gender indication precision, keeping other factors constant, and find that the ease of grammar determines the baseline accuracy of gender prediction, and that the difference in baseline accuracy between speakers is largely determined by language differences rather than individual differences. Our study reveals that larger learning datasets do not guarantee improved precision in lower-predictability languages. To bridge the knowledge gap about the effect of education on human language abilities, we suggest developing simple, computationally assisted 'language games' that automatically evaluate and compare how speakers utilize word meanings to indicate grammatical gender in various languages. Our training data and associated code are publicly available at https://github.com/matteosoratici/gender_in_practice.

Estimating the pose of objects in situations where there is a large number of
different objects poses an significant challenge. Traditional approaches rely on
large amounts of annotated training data, which becomes impractical once new
items are added. We've explored two solutions to this problem: one involves
training networks without annotations, while the other utilises pose annotations
in a semi-supervised manner by leveraging unannotated images. We've tested
these methods and compared them to other available techniques. The code used
in this research can be accessed at https://github.com/auricchio/zero-shot-pose.

Predicting short-term traffic flows helps us prepare for various scenarios.
However, existing traffic forecasting models face significant challenges due
to limited historical data and irregular sparsity in traffic sequences. To
address these issues, we present a novel sparse traffic forecasting framework
focusing on extensive sparse traffic patterns. We introduce a data augmentation
approach to process the irregular sparsity in traffic data by representing it
as a multi-temporal and multi-scale phenomenon. Then, we design a similarity-
driven feature extraction algorithm to identify patterns in traffic patterns by
using similar traffic data as reference points. We also use point processes to
model the irregular sparsity in traffic sequences and propose a neural network
based training algorithm to train the model. We evaluate our approach by
conducting experiments on two datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in
traffic prediction compared to other conventional methods. Additionally, we
apply our approach to universal prediction tasks and achieve improved results.

The film industry's success relies heavily on determining the potential earnings of a movie. Predicting this gross income upon its initial release can be a crucial factor in informing decisions made by film studios, investors, and distributors. Various characteristics of a movie are examined in this paper to see if any can accurately forecast its box office revenue in a straightforward manner. A new comprehensive film dataset, consisting of 517 films and totaling 9 million viewers, was used to carry out these investigations. Our analysis is then expanded across a broader Chinar Film dataset comprising 205 movies and 7.5 million viewers. Our study reveals that movie traits such as inflation, the number of stars, the volume of the opening scene, and the length of a movie are significant contributing factors in estimating its box office revenue. Moreover, a unique model was developed that utilizes a combination of inflation and movie traits as a predictor of earnings, resulting in a predicted random error of the sample size multiplied by 0.24, showing improved accuracy compared to the commonly used model of Ebert's Law. The latter has a predicted random error of the sample size multiplied by 0.48. In addition, a graphical representation of a movie's opening scene from a center point is also examined, resulting in the discovery that movie traits such as inflation and the length of a movie's opening scene from a center point are sufficient predictors of its box office revenue, resulting in a predicted random error of the sample size multiplied by 0.48. The proposed method was also compared with the regression model of Ebert's Law. Our study reveals that Chinar films have a lower predicted random error of 0.17, while 28% fewer predictors are used. These findings highlight that the characteristics of a movie such as its opening scene are pivotal in estimating its box office revenue, making them a worthwhile area of investigation for film studios and investors to consider. The new film dataset is available on GitHub at https://github.com/AliMirzaChopan/Chinar-Film. The necessary programming code for this research is available on https://github.com/AliMirzaChopan/Chinar-Film/tree/main/BoxOfficePrediction. The growing integration of distributed power sources into modern electricity grids poses significant challenges to voltage stability. Traditionally, centralized power systems maintained stable voltage levels through a surplus of capacity, but with the rise of renewable energy, the increased variability often leads to voltage fluctuations. As a result, the capacity for supporting stable voltage levels in increasingly decentralized power systems is continually depleted. Research has identified auxiliary frequency regulation as a potential stabilizing force, particularly in response to the rapid changes in power supply and demand. Testing has been conducted on an open-loop model of a power system, rather than a dynamic one, to evaluate the influence of AFC on minimizing voltage fluctuations. While the actual impact of AFC on a real power grid is difficult to determine due to a lack of real-world data, the technique has been found to significantly outperform other control methods in stabilizing voltage levels. Notably, the 2020 Solar Power Integration Study by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory provided estimates for the power output of solar photovoltaic cells. Similarly, the Advanced Materials Aronimut Model, developed by the University of Vermont, predicted the social behavior of solar panel owners. This information can be utilized to simulate various power systems and measure the effect of different control methods, such as AFC, on voltage stability. Simulation results indicate that AFC is highly effective in stabilizing voltage levels, particularly in decentralized power systems, by rapidly adjusting to changes in power supply and demand. In fact, the technique demonstrated the capacity to maintain stable voltage levels with as little as 5% of the conventional frequency regulation resources, far lower than the 90% typically required in centralized power systems. Moreover, the results show that AFC outperforms other control methods such as SLHC and PQ in stabilizing voltage levels, while the performance differences between AFC and the conventional frequency regulation resources, FF, are particularly pronounced in scenarios with high solar integration. Specifically, the technique has been found to reduce peak voltage fluctuations by more than 30% in scenarios with 50% solar integration, while the integration of solar power above 80% has been found to yield the greatest improvements in voltage stability. In contrast, the performance differences between AFC and the conventional frequency regulation resources, FF, are particularly pronounced in scenarios with high demand variability. Specifically, the technique has been found to reduce minimum and mean voltage levels by more than 10% and 5%, respectively, in scenarios with 60% demand variability. The classical Vitushin extension, primarily relied upon in numerical analysis, is inherently limited in applying data points that aren't evenly spaced on a grid due to its inherent interlacing structure. In order to overcome this limitation, a new approach called the analytical extension with complex supports is introduced in this paper. This innovation enables the construction of a Cauchy-type integral formula tailored for use on irregular domains with the potential for points on a general Riemann surface to be included in the new extension. Consequently, the new approach eliminates the need for points on a grid to be interlaced and thus provides a more versatile tool. To demonstrate its feasibility and efficiency, the new extension is verified through its application in a high-order finite element method on complex polyhedra described by Cauchy-type reproducing kernel operators. Performance is evaluated in two ways: first through a model problem on a domain with a star-shaped mesh where the new extension outperforms its interlaced counterpart; secondly, to further the development of geometric finite element methods, an example is provided on a geometric polygon with curved boundaries featuring a least-squares type discretization where the new extension exhibits superior performance compared to its interlaced counterpart. Implementation details, including assembly procedures, are provided in order to further illustrate the new extension's feasibility and efficiency in practice. Further research into its broader implications and applications is recommended. The related MATLAB code is freely accessible online at the author's homepage. Upon reviewing the code, it becomes apparent that the new extension's analysis can be further expanded to encompass a broader range of topics such as adaptive refinement, curved geometries, and generalized geometric operators, suggesting a bright future for its development and implementation. Upon initial deployment in a geometric finite element library called geometric-element, a notable speedup of approximately three times is observed compared to its previous version that only supported interlaced discretizations. Consequently, the new extension's analysis and implementation serve as an excellent proof-of-concept, paving the way for its seamless integration in practice to further broaden its capabilities and applications in numerical analysis and computational science. A novel approach to explaining baryon generation in quantum chromodynamics has been proposed, centered on a QCD field excited within a quantized, fragmented, and helical solar plasma filaments. This theory establishes a paradigm for non-topological symmetry breaking, thereby creating baryons from the vacuum. Initially, the QCD field is stimulated by a color charge, subsequently transitioning into a state of instability. As the QCD field continues to grow, it breaks up into separate regions, each featuring distinct color charge states, causing the initial charge to diminish. When the QCD field settles into a state of equilibrium within each region, it transforms from a state of excitation to a state of quark and gluon confinement, thereby giving rise to baryons, which inhabit regions of varying scales. Multiple baryons can emerge from a single measurement volume, and given that the solar plasma filaments exhibit a spiral shape, the generation of baryons is naturally linked to the properties of the solar magnetic field. This theory offers an innovative solution to explaining baryon generation and could potentially provide a new and broader understanding of the underlying physical processes within the universe. The $\Sigma^+ \to \pi^+ \mu^+ \mu^-$ transition is examined in the context of hadronic light-by-light contributions to $(g-2)_\mu$.
Our calculation, which uses chiral perturbation theory, considers general form factors for the rare decays $\Sigma^+ \to \pi^+ \gamma$, $\Sigma^+ \to \pi^+ \gamma_5$, and $\Sigma^+ \to \pi^- \bar{\nu}_\mu$, then applies these form factors to $\Sigma^+ \to p \gamma$, $\Sigma^+ \to p \gamma_5$, and $\Sigma^+ \to p \bar{\nu}_\mu$ with the relativistic quark formalism.
These form factors are subsequently used in the hadronic light-by-light diagram for the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ transition, yielding a cross-section of 1.0 fb for the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^- $ process via the $\gamma \rightarrow \pi^0, \eta, \eta'$ mechanism.
Our calculation also finds that the $\Sigma^+ \to n \mu^+ \mu^-$ transition has a vanishing amplitude.
Therefore, it is concluded that the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ transition can be observed at the LHCb experiment with the condition that the $\Sigma^+$ be produced and identified. 
Our study provides the first comprehensive theoretical estimate for the rare transition $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$. 
It is anticipated that the forthcoming data from the LHCb experiment will confirm this prediction and thus verify the rare transition.
Our work has also been implemented as a C++ program and made freely available via GitHub. 
Our code can be run as a standalone application to generate plots and compute probabilities for rare transitions in hadronic processes involving muons and baryons. 
It is envisioned that the code may be utilized in future investigations on baryonic light-by-light contributions to the muon anomalous magnetic moment or other rare hadronic transitions.

This paper explores a wireless recharging network consisting of a source node, an intelligent surface, recharging nodes, and devices. The source node transmits a signal to the intelligent surface, which in turn reflects it to the recharging nodes. The recharging nodes then use energy harvesting to continue receiving signals from the source node after their initial energy depletion. Due to the presence of an obstructing node, the source node's signal strength is affected, which is modeled using the Rayleigh fading model. A machine learning method is proposed to address this uncertainty. A neural network is trained to optimize system performance, allowing it to predict the optimal system performance even when the obstructing node's signal strength is unknown. Furthermore, a novel unsupervised learning approach is proposed to address cases where the obstructing node's parameters cannot be estimated. The performance of this approach is compared with existing solutions in literature. Results show that the proposed method can reduce the total system energy consumption by up to 25% compared to other reference methods in literature. The method's efficacy is evaluated through several simulation scenarios under different conditions, such as varying sizes of the recharging network and the obstructing node. The unsupervised learning method's performance improvements are most noticeable in scenarios where the size of the recharging network is small and the obstructing node is close to the recharging nodes. However, the method's performance degradation at higher bandwidths can be attributed to the discrepancy between the real and the learned channel gain matrices. evaluation of translation reliability with unbiased translation assessment,

This work presents our three-stage solution for the domain adaptation problem in the context of object classification. Building on recent advancements, we leverage a transient feature space bridge consisting of self-attention modules and pre-trained models such as SwAV and CLIP to connect the source and target domains. A novel approach involves constructing a bridge with two parallel networks: one designed for bridge construction and extraction, and the other for reducing domain gaps. We evaluated the bridge's effectiveness by implementing various strategies in the two-stage and three-stage settings. Notably, we obtained first and second places in four and three one-shot domain adaptation challenges, respectively, with the three-stage setting exhibiting superior performance across all tested domains. Furthermore, we achieved a mean adaptation ratio of 72.4% using our three-stage solution without employing target domain training. By combining our method with additional supervision from multiple bridges, we obtained an adaptation ratio of 73.6%. Our results significantly outperform previous state-of-the-art methods, and the proposed technique allows for the construction of a bridge without modification to pre-trained models or domain-specific training. The Strauss process is a point process, and its density is uncomputable, so it's typically simulated through a mixture representation, combining a Poisson point process and, in each cluster, independently generating points up to a maximum radius. However, this mixture representation experiences two issues: first, simulating such a point process accurately proves challenging because generating points independently within a given radius only ensures they fall in the same cluster, but not necessarily in the given area, and second, even if the points are in the area, they might not form a connected cluster. To address these problems, we suggest a new simulation method for the Strauss model, based on stitching together areas with dense point clusters. We start by selecting areas with dense point clusters, then stitching them together to form the ultimate set of clusters. We simulate the point patterns in each area independently from a Poisson process, and connect these areas by merging these patterns into a single point pattern. We propose an algorithm that, given any parameter beta, efficiently simulates the Strauss model and provides accurate estimates of the model's parameters. Notably, our simulated models align closely with theoretically simulated models, and the method is efficient, usable online, and free. We applied this method to a well-known dataset of shooting stars, and the results show that it provides reliable estimates of the model's parameters. Furthermore, the method is efficient, taking less than 0.01 seconds to simulate the model and providing reliable estimates of the model's parameters in just three simulations. We provide visual evidence of the method's effectiveness in Figure 1 and Figure 2, and the code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/yuskywki/Strauss-Model-stitching. We conclude that the Strauss model is not a good fit for the dataset of shooting stars, and the point process might be better modelled through a different distribution, such as the Bartlett or Gaussian distribution, especially given the significant negative correlation observed in the dataset's density. To address these issues, we suggest a different way to stitch together the clusters in order to capture the observed correlation in the dataset's density. In various theoretical frameworks such as string theory, loop quantum gravity, and Amelino-Cambiaso theories, the concept of generalized uncertainty principles has emerged, challenging the validity of classical space-time. These GUP models predict a nonlinear modification to the momentum operator within quantum mechanics. This work explores the effects of this transformation on the energy spectrum of a free particle and the conditions necessary for the emergence of a novel Lorentz factor in these GUP models. To achieve this, we utilize the GUP momentum operator in the Schrödinger equation for a free particle, obtaining the corresponding wave functions and energy spectra. As a result, we identify three scenarios that could potentially lead to the emergence of these GUP alterations: the GUP must either introduce time dilation in the Galilean group or a combination of time and space dilation in the Lorentz group. Furthermore, we establish the connections between the GUP models and previously existing alterations. Additionally, we outline the conditions and constraints for transitioning from the Minkowski space to a different GUP alteration and discuss the potential implications of the GUP models on quantum mechanics in the context of recent experiments. This work explores two primary scenarios: the GUP model in the context of the Schrödinger equation for a free particle, as well as the Klein-Gordon and Dirac equations, which could potentially be applied to the study of quantum mechanics. However, we find that the GUP models and their resulting energy spectra may not be compatible with recent experiments, particularly those involving the scattering of electrons on cesium nuclei. Nevertheless, we identify an exceptional scenario in which the GUP models and their resulting energy spectra may not be testable with conventional means. Finally, we provide an assessment of the validity and potential applications of these GUP models. The present study aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the GUP models and their potential connections to the emergence of relativistic effects, as well as their implications for quantum mechanics and the principles of space-time alterations. Furthermore, this work aims to explore the GUP models and their potential applications in detail, resulting in a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between these models and the emergence of relativistic effects. The GUP models and their potential applications are further studied in a companion paper. In this paper, we introduce the Multitasking Timetabling problem as a suitable model for navigating real-world concurrency challenges into a high-stress, time-constrained environment. Our objective is to optimize a solution strategy for a task list divided among agents working concurrently, allowing them to share processing power as needed. To achieve this, we outline a range of policies for managing concurrent work and share experimental results demonstrating their effectiveness in varied sequential and concurrent scenarios. Additionally, we provide practical guidelines for choosing a shared processing strategy and offer a decision-making framework to facilitate this process. Our collaborative approach yields better outcomes than a solo problem-solving approach, as demonstrated through experiments comparing the performance of multiple task management methods across multiple processing scenarios. The MTMT framework is applicable to a range of task management methodologies, including reduction and approximation methods, as illustrated through its successful application to the classic Two-Machines Problem with a bounded job-dependent processing limit. Our collaborative approach yields significant reductions in computational time, significantly outperforming a comprehensive scanning strategy that exhaustively evaluates all possible processing configurations to ensure optimal results. In particular, for a fixed time limit of 40 seconds, the proposed shared processing strategy yields solutions of high quality (less than 3% above optimal) while simultaneously reducing the search time by at least 20%, or at most 85% (with respect to a comprehensive scanning strategy that may not always find the optimal solution). The MTMT framework is available as an open-source library called multitasking-timetabling. The MTMT repository contains further details regarding the experimental setup, including the two processing methodologies we use to evaluate the shared processing strategy's effectiveness in a range of concurrent scenarios. To the best of our knowledge, this work constitutes a pioneering approach to using shared processing power to improve task management efficiency in a real-world, stress-filled environment. Unfortunately, the majority of current systems do not facilitate this capability, resulting in the potential for vulnerabilities to persist forever. The implementation of reliable and verified update mechanisms is essential to enabling after-market security enhancements. In our research, we thoroughly evaluated the trustworthiness of Wi-Fi mesh networks, which provide the key features necessary for large-scale IoT update implementations. By using these updates, it's possible for an IoT device to be amended to a trusted version, even if it was initially compromised. In our experiments, we successfully and reliably updated 30 mesh nodes and 5 gateway evaluations, with the fastest update finishing in 12 seconds and the longest taking 40 seconds. In total, we conducted 57 successful updates, with a failed update occurring only once after initiating the update process on the gateway. In addition, we examined the resilience of updates in environments with interference and interjected excessive network problems, resulting in a successful update outcome in all instances. In addition, we tested the security of the network by simulating an adversary's attack and found the network to be secure, with the adversary failing to disrupt the updates at least once. In total, we conducted a comprehensive analysis encompassing 16 meshes and 5 gateway evaluations, with a combined total of 57 successful updates to the network. The problem of target search by interactive cost function estimation is well defined with a target characterised by an unknown function. An agent must take actions, estimate the target's characterisation state, and make decisions on whether to continue at a cost, aiming to find the target by limiting the total cost. This paper generalises existing work on searching for a single target to the case where multiple targets exist, each modelled by an unknown function. A Bayesian search strategy is proposed, and we provide a lower bound on the minimal expected cost for a Bayesian agent to find at least one target. Furthermore, a semi-realtime budget limited algorithm is proposed, and we demonstrate its performance by comparing it to a Bayesian agent under a simulation in a two-dimensional space. A thorough analysis of this algorithm's limitations is also presented. Finally, we discuss how this algorithm's limitations could be overcome in a semi-supervised learning framework. An additional experiment demonstrates that in a learning scenario, we can achieve improved results compared to the Bayesian agent. The performance of our algorithm is linked to the concept of epsilon-regexes, and we discuss the challenges of learning such regexes from data. We conclude with suggestions on potential approaches to overcome the challenges identified. An accompanying technical report contains additional material. Our investigation delves into the adversarial domain by introducing conceptually straightforward yet challenging cases of input manipulation that can trick quantum classifiers. We demonstrate that adversarial instances exist in both classical and quantum environments and provide theoretical frameworks for generating them through optimization techniques. In the context of power network expansion, a fundamental issue arises: 
Given the current network and future projections of demand and generation capacity, 
What is the preferred location and capacity for adding transmission lines, overhead cables, and other infrastructure?

This paper poses the same question within the context of network synthesis, a problem initially solved by the Karsten circulation method.
A new approach based on vector potentials has been proposed, enabling the formulation of a linear system that can be solved consistently.
Despite its consistent linearity, the new approach yields more accurate results for real-world scenarios than nonlinear methods.
Furthermore, our study exposes a critical factor that affects the accuracy of power network expansion models.
Notably, our approach based on vector potentials offers a scalable solution for large-scale problems, in contrast to the Karsten circulation method which suffers from numerical limitations.
We have demonstrated the efficacy of our method by applying it to the American Midwest power network and the French electricity grid.
Our results show that network infrastructure optimization significantly reduces the material and economic costs incurred.
Additionally, our approach enables the identification of specific characteristics, namely, the condition number of the network and the leverage effect of new infrastructure on existing infrastructure.
We have concluded that our method has the potential to significantly influence power network expansion planning in real-world scenarios. 
This paper is particularly relevant due to recent investments in renewable energy and grid modernization, 
Which our approach can effectively accommodate and utilize, as shown in our empirical results. 
In particular, our results show that our method can minimize the material and economic costsincurred in power network infrastructure development. 
Unfortunately, our initial application of our method to the South France power grid was marred by numerical issues due to the complexity of the network.

Research venues play a crucial role in evaluating the quality of research. However, current metrics, heavily relying on citations, are inadequate in assessing venues, particularly those hosting up-to-date workshops and conferences. We propose 'Venue Insights', a set of quantitative and qualitative indicators that can provide a comprehensive view of a venue's quality, more accurately than citations can. Our framework offers several key metrics, including 'Venue Insights', 'Article Insights', and 'Author Productivity', all designed to offer insight into a venue's performance. We 'crawled' relevant data from top research fields and analyzed it, examining the effectiveness of our proposed metrics in evaluating venues. Our results show that, by using a combination of our metrics, it is possible to accurately predict a venue's H-index, much like how citations can. To further validate our approach, we also demonstrated its ability to identify top-tier venues, even in research fields where our method was initially untrained. Notably, our method produced results comparable to those obtained by trained models, shedding light on the role of citations in identifying top venues. Our work is publicly available at https://github.com/massalag/ VenueInsights/, aiming to facilitate the evaluation of research quality and the assessment of a venue's reputation. As such, our method could be utilized in various applications, from supporting scientific decision-making to informing strategic venue selections, thereby aiding both individuals and organizations in making more informed choices. Ultimately, our results illustrate the value of our proposed Venue Insights, serving as a reliable and accurate alternative to traditional citation-based metrics for evaluating a venue's quality. Moreover, our method, being easily adaptable to other fields, can be readily scaled up, allowing us to confidently expect similar outcomes if the analysis were to be applied to research published after 2020, while our model could also be applied to analyze a broader range of research quality metrics beyond just citations. In the field of control engineering, identifying trustworthy artificial neural networks (ANNs) is crucial, especially as they start being integrated into control systems. The main obstacles to including ANNs in control loops involve a lack of methods to validate their reliability. The key factors to consider are that ANNs can learn patterns in data but not provide explanations for their predictions, a concern known as explainability. Furthermore, ANNs can only rely on data consistency, a concern known as identifiability. This study aims to develop a framework that addresses these issues by learning an ANN that mimics a control system's behavior without explicitly providing the design parameters. The system in question features a nonlinear plant with a nonlinear controller, with both components subject to performance limitations defined by performance indices. The key components of this framework involve a first approach using optimization techniques to identify whether it's possible to achieve the desired control objectives based on a set of given constraints and data. Another part of this framework involves a method that trains ANNs while accounting for the constraints of the data and ensures that the learned controller meets the desired performance standards by perfectly replicating the plant's behavior for its entire operating range. The first method is known as constraint propagation for identifiability and is based on a type of machine learning called symbolic regression, while the second involves reinforcement learning. We will also provide an example that demonstrates how to implement this framework by focusing on a system that uses a controller with a controller area network constraint in order to achieve the desired control objectives. This is because the standard nonlinear Coulomb-phase-integral analysis is insufficient for the high power levels of these systems. The challenge of sparse network representation is particularly difficult to tackle due to its inherent data characteristics. Consequently, existing methods are either tailored to complete networks or those with a moderate level of sparsity. However, these approaches pose significant drawbacks when applied to sparse networks. For instance, using a neighborhood size that is too large results in the loss of critical edge and node data. On the other hand, a neighborhood size that is too small fails to adequately encode structural information. 

Building upon the foundations of node representation, a novel, efficient approach called SSNE is proposed. This method utilizes a stochastic gradient descent framework in conjunction with random walk, incorporating both local and global structural information via the employment of multiple neighborhood sizes. In doing so, SSNE effectively mitigates the impact of data sparsity through the enhancement of node embeddings using multiple size gradients. 

SSNE's efficacy is demonstrated on numerous network types, yielding superior link prediction performance when compared to various baseline approaches. Experimental findings also highlight the advantages of SSNE over competing node representation frameworks from the fields of node, link, and community prediction. Moreover, a comprehensive analysis of SSNE is provided, exploring such topics as hyperparameter sensitivity, the influence of the random walk on SSNE node representations, and its application to networks of varying sizes. This study ultimately showcases SSNE's ability to effectively handle networks of a wide range of sparsity and size. Early detection and treatment of depression is essential to prevent severe mental health progression and decrease mortality risks by intervening in high-risk individuals.  The emergence of Social Media has provided an opportunity to gather vast amounts of data on online user behavior, enabling researchers to identify indicative patterns of depression through computational analysis.  A vast dataset of nearly 20,000 Social Media posts was compiled, along with detailed clinical information regarding authors' mental health status. Every post was annotated as being either depressive or non-depressive. Two distinct datasets were created for training and testing purposes. When trained on one set of data and tested on another, a machine learning model performed consistently, achieving an 82% accuracy rating. Consequently, this model successfully identified depressive content with 91% accuracy and non-depressive content with 80% accuracy when tested against independent data. Such findings highlight the feasibility of utilizing AI-powered tools for detecting indications of depression from Social Media posts not only in one culture but also across multiple populations by overcoming language barriers through the use of a machine translation. Furthermore, these results show that depression detection is not only applicable to individuals but also to diverse population groups. Training data from various population groups is essential for expanding detection capabilities to broader audiences. In the field of reinforcement learning and qualitative hedging, a significant concern exists regarding the bias inherent in value function estimation techniques, particularly when used in association with hedging strategies in quantitative finance. The objective of our research is to address this issue by developing an innovative method for estimating the optimal hedging cost with minimal inherent bias. By combining Proximal Gradient Smoothing, a sophisticated smoothing technique, and leveraging characteristics of convex optimization, we establish the viability of utilizing deep neural networks to approximate key components of a partial differential equation that governs the optimal hedging cost, thereby enabling the derivation of a bias-reduced estimator. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our proposed estimator converges at an efficient rate and showcase its efficacy through successful implementations in both synthetic and real-world scenarios. The latter involves hedging options on cryptocurrencies, a task which we successfully accomplish with low inherent bias in the case of noisy data. By utilizing our biased-but-efficient estimation method in conjunction with statistical inference techniques, we are able to obtain reliable estimates of the optimal hedging cost, thus complementing our partial derivative equation estimation results. Notably, our findings highlight the presence of stochastic components in the data generation process, a fact established through the analysis of the distribution of the sample-mean estimator of the optimal hedging cost, showing convergence at an efficient rate. The eco-evolutionary process is driven by interconnected feedback loops involving ecological structures and genetic information. These interactions are influenced by various processes such as natural selection, genetic drift, and ecological changes. Early developments in eco-evolutionary dynamics were characterized by a deterministic approach, as evident from the "modern" eco-evolutionary dynamics framework introduced by Odling-Smither et al. (2020). This framework highlighted the similarities between short-term and long-term dynamics, supported by the concept of quasi-linear systems. This work presents an extensive expansion of the framework, additional insights into eco-evolutionary dynamics, and mathematical proofs of the stability across different time scales. Moreover, we separate deterministic and probabilistic drivers of eco-evolutionary dynamics and show that probabilistic forces can lead to drastic changes in dynamics when applied to individual organisms. These findings emphasize the significance of understanding scale dependencies, rate modifiers, and data availability when studying eco-evolutionary processes. They also lead to new research directions, such as reinterpreting drift's influence or applying eco-evolutionary dynamics to the understanding of COVID-19 dynamics. This work serves as a comprehensive resource for both theoretical studies on scalar dependencies and applicable research on drift, highlighting the importance of data-driven eco-evolutionary investigations. It is hoped that this work will inspire future research on the scaling of ecological and genetic modifiers as well as the exploration of an entirely new class of systems that are both linear and non-linear. The advantages of large-scale pretraining have been consistently confirmed in speaker-independent tasks, yet this approach may undermine speaker diversity and create difficulties in pronunciation. To explore the negative effects of pretraining models on speech quality, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation from two perspectives. Firstly, we developed a role-playing test to investigate whether there's a connection between a model's ability to distinguish speakers and its impaired pronunciation performance. Secondly, we examined the impact of pronunciation difficulties and the effectiveness of pronunciation correction methods on pretraining models. Our results demonstrate that previously learned speaker distinction skills do not significantly influence a model's speech quality. Additionally, we found that pronunciation errors in pretraining models are due to the neglect of local context in self-supervised learning and can be mitigated by incorporating pronunciation correction into pretraining. Our findings highlight the importance of validating pretraining models and integrating speech quality into pretraining frameworks to improve model performance. Our code and data are available on GitHub at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/SigmapiNas. 

Keywords: speech quality, speaker distinction, pretraining, pronunciation errors, role-playing test, speaker-dependent tasks. 

From a pretraining perspective, our study identifies the speech quality issue as a significant challenge that needs to be addressed. Existing approaches have documented the advantages of pretraining models but have not thoroughly explored the negative effects on speech quality. Our findings provide concrete evidence of the speech quality problem and suggest that a model's speaker distinction ability does not directly contribute to its speech quality. We also suggest that pronunciation errors in pretraining models are a result of the neglect of local context in self-supervised learning and can be mitigated through the incorporation of pronunciation correction. 

The main limitations of our study are that they are evaluated by a human subject and not by a machine. Moreover, our suggestions for addressing the speech quality issue are based on a post-hoc analysis and not a systematic search. Finally, our ideas have not been tested in other settings and require further replication. 

The contributions of our study can be summarized as follows: 

  We have characterized the hostile susceptibility of pretraining models and identified speech quality as a crucial performance metric. We have also developed a role-playing test to investigate the connection between a model's speaker distinction skills and its pronunciation performance. 

  We have looked at the impact of pronunciation difficulties and the effectiveness of pronunciation correction methods on pretraining models and proposed incorporating pronunciation correction into pretraining frameworks to improve model performance. 

  We have based our study on a pretraining pipeline and have not considered other pipelines.

A new framework called the E-value was introduced to address the uncertainty associated with these cases by providing a clear measure of how reliable inferences based on incomplete data can be. This paper focuses on how the E-value works in Bayesian contexts, particularly when missing data is an issue. To illustrate this point, a number of examples are used, including one very simple scenario where a hypothesis test is in question. Furthermore, a complex case involving the analysis of incomplete data from an assorted set of sources is also examined to demonstrate the capabilities of the E-value in such complex data sets, including when missing data is not random in origin. Despite these capabilities, the E-value does have some limitations that become particularly apparent when trying to determine the extent to which the results are affected by missing data in question - a challenge the researchers addressed by developing a novel Bayesian method to help quantify these effects, or lack thereof, and thereby providing a measure of how the results derived from incomplete data are influenced by them. To validate the developed method, a number of synthetic and real-world data sets are consulted and the researchers also provide suggestions for how the results can be further refined. abuses, such as Bitcoinabuse and Ethereumabuse, focusing solely on those platforms.
In this research paper, we examine the broader spectrum of abusive activity 
surrounding Python crypto libraries and discuss how such abuse compares to previous
findings. To achieve this, we gathered data from 12 stealer families along with
4000 malicious clips from ClipMix, a CLIP-based universal prompt-based model.
The results of our study show that Python crypto libraries continue to be favored by
malware authors, with certain libraries being targeted by multiple families.
Furthermore, our ClipMix model reveals that crypto-related abuses comprise 44.2% 
of, and payments constitute 13.1% of, all malicious requests stemming from such
abuses. Notably, our study also indicates that payment-instructions are frequently
repeated in requests. The prominent use of Python crypto libraries by malware authors
is likely due to their cross-platform compatibility. The success of payment-related 
abuses might be attributed to the lack of appropriate guidance provided to 
malware authors, as evidenced by the high proportion of prompts containing 
instructions to steal cryptocurrencies (43.8%) in our dataset. This study's results 
could be utilized to enhance the accuracy of cryptocurrency recovery in the event of

Seismic data is currently the sole largest source of unstructured data within geosciences, and its analysis has far-reaching implications for geoscience and potential oil reserves.  The underlying mechanics of geophysical processes cause significant nonuniform sparse patterns in geophysical data, and ignoring these characteristics or applying uniform sparse methods results in the underestimation of data accuracy.  A new approach, called NuSPAN, is the first to effectively model these complex nonuniform dependencies and has been successfully applied to the reconstruction of seismic reflectivity using partial stack amplitude information.  The results show that NuSPAN outperforms the alternative Sparsity-based Partial Stack Amlitude inversion method by a significant margin, with estimated residual norms decreasing to the order of ten-thousandths, whereas Sparsity-based Partial Stack Amlitude inversion could only decrease to the order of ten-thousands.  The observed differences are largely attributed to NuSPAN's enhanced data fitting capabilities and accelerated convergence rates.  A comparative analysis using the established Gamma2D seismic synthetic model reveals that NuSPAN's convergence iterations are dramatically reduced - from 95 times using the original proposed method to 17 times using the proposed method, thereby substantially shortening the total computational time.  The proposed method is also shown to effectively handle high-frequency data components and can be used as a model for diverse tasks beyond seismic reconstruction.  The implemented code for NuSPAN is provided as open-source software.  A comprehensive framework for the numerical model used in this research, including both seismic inversion and deep learning components, is made available through the TerraFirma-MLAB GitHub repository as open-source software.  The provided repository includes the code for the numerical model used in this research, including the model itself, the Sparsity-based Partial Stack Amplitude Inversion method used for comparison, and the open-source software enabling the model to run as a standalone, severless, and parallel application for seismic inversion. In linguistics, part-of-speech annotation is a crucial task that has been largely neglected when dealing with historical languages, due to the labor-intensive nature of manual correction. Unlike modern languages, where machine-learned models can effectively identify parts of speech, historical corpora pose a problem due to the significant differences in writing styles, vocabulary, and grammar. To overcome this challenge, we suggest combining traditional machine learning with a method of set-valued prediction, initially developed for forecasting uncertain electrical loads. By employing this set-valued prediction method in HANSZ, we can accurately identify the probable parts of speech in historical texts, even when the training data is limited. In addition to addressing the issue of pos label noise, our approach also accounts for the variability in writing style across documents. Experimental results for HANSZ demonstrate that the set-valued prediction method is effective in providing more accurate pos predictions, ultimately leading to enhanced syntactic parsing. Notably, the pos errors in Hansz corpus have been reduced from 26.1% to 12.9%, while the english bison scores have been improved from 44.9% to 64.9%. Furthermore, we have also made our code available for public access, providing other researchers with the opportunity to adapt this method for other historical corpora. The code can be found at https://github.com/alijimgroup/set-valued-poselection.

To facilitate easier comprehension, the text includes numerous illustrative examples and, as a practical demonstration of NUI's utility, includes a comprehensive examination of classical and modern methods for deriving coercive estimates in elliptic PDEs. Moreover, the text synthesizes various NUI-related results and theories, including the relative compactness of bounded sequences in L^2 and W^{1,p}, as well as the applicability of the Banach-Alaoglu Theorem to derive weak convergence principles. As a bonus, the text includes a review of NUI-based approaches to the study of homogenization problems for elliptic operators with high contrast. All mathematical definitions, theorems, and findings presented in this review are formally incorporated into an extensive theoretical framework dubbed Non-Uniform Integrability Theory. This framework consists of 23 distinct objects, including definitions, propositions, and theorems, which are grouped into six chapters, each with an accompanying example and a bibliography containing over 200 primary references. This study presents a novel approach to correct quantum errors called the concealed inverses protocol (CIP). This protocol leverages the unique properties of post-secondary gates in a control-qubit qubit system to efficiently correct quantum errors without increased dispersion and subsequently restore the encoded state with high fidelity. Through analysis using the fidelity formula, our findings demonstrate that the CIP is adaptable to various quantum error models and remains efficient when modified to accommodate a higher code rate or encodings of increased depth. Furthermore, our experimental investigation utilizing a superconducting quantum apparatus revealed that the CIP can effectively mitigate errors and maintain high fidelity during the encoding process. This protocol offers a versatile error correction strategy with wide-ranging applications. Using the quantum circuit simulator (QCS) software package, our research delves into the theoretical foundations of CIP in qubit systems, and experiments were conducted in a superconducting quantum apparatus to validate its practical efficacy in real-world applications. To efficiently deploy CIP in practical scenarios, our team developed a framework comprising two key components: the CIP-based CNOT pool and the priority queue with dynamic priority assignment. This approach ensures that CIP can correct errors in a superconducting quantum apparatus to achieve high fidelity encoding. Our research introduces a new cost model to optimize CIP-driven encoding for a specific number of repetitions and a given quantum circuit. By combining CIP with CNOT pool and queue strategies, our team can dynamically manage and adjust the priority assignment based on current conditions in a superconducting quantum apparatus, thereby allowing us to efficiently utilize CIP in practical scenarios. We start by examining the surface term for Einstein's equations and demonstrate that a specific complex disorder, equivalent in value to the Lichnerowicz scalar, must be incorporated to ensure that the Noether charge of the surface term remains well-defined. This is because the Noether charge, which emerges from Noether's theorem when considering a surface term based on general relativity, is initially ill-defined due to a divergent variation. After adding this specific complex disorder, we obtain a well-defined variation, which in turn enables us to identify the Noether charge as a complex generalisation of the Holst charge. Finally, we endeavour to identify a Hamiltonian vector field corresponding to time-shifts, which would be necessary for forming a Virasoro algebra through Poisson brackets. Although we are unable to conclusively identify this vector field, we are able to conclude that, for certain disorders, the Noether equation can be expressed in a form similar to the Virasoro equation, which in turn suggests that the corresponding Noether charge remains well-defined even in the absence of any disorder. This Noether charge can then be used as the generator of time-shifts, which in turn enables us to identify a corresponding Hamiltonian vector field and complete the closure of the Virasoro algebra through Poisson brackets. This is, however, found to only be possible for disorders that are conformally invariant. A concise overview of related material from the context of general relativity and differential topology is also included in the appendix for the reader's convenience. Despite our best efforts, we are unable to fully address the corresponding Hamiltonian vector field and the topological aspects relevant to the Hamiltonian generalised on the Kugo-Klein model, which remains an outstanding problem for general relativity. Regional queries, which involve learning from multiple instances within a given dataset subset, are contrasted with incremental learning, which entails learning instance-by-instance. We introduce a novel metric to measure regional query helpfulness and establish conditions under which regional queries are more helpful than incremental learning. We also gather empirical results demonstrating that regional queries are advantageous in various machine learning scenarios, such as text categorization and hyper-spectral image classification. Moreover, our findings indicate that regional queries are beneficial when there is relative entropy between the target and source distributions. We also show that incremental learning is beneficial when there is sufficient target data availability, which is not the case in most machine learning scenarios. Overall, our results suggest that regional queries are more helpful than incremental learning in various learning environments. Our previous research found that utilizing a binary binary search framework in computing the optimal transport gap function led to an O(n log n) time complexity. Building upon this foundation, we have made a significant further contribution by establishing that key optimal transport parameters can be computed in O(n) time by exploiting the characteristics of binary matrices. Specifically, we demonstrate that iterating through the rows of such a matrix can be performed in O(n) time, which is the basis for deriving several valuable results, including an explicit formula for the optimal transport gradient. Moreover, we have developed a new algorithm for computing optimal transport weights in O(n) time, which is accompanied by a high-accuracy approximation method for the optimal transport matrix. Interestingly, the efficacy of our new algorithm is illustrated by its ability to achieve accurate results even with a precision of O(1/n) in a wide range of tests. Furthermore, we have shown that our new algorithm can be modified to work with complex matrices, while also providing two enhanced versions that achieve even faster performance by leveraging parallel processing capabilities provided by GPUs. Finally, we have demonstrated the applicability of our algorithm to real-world applications by successfully using it to process large-scale optimal transport problems involving high-resolution image datasets. Specifically, we have applied our algorithm to compute optimal transport maps for pairs of 1024x1024 images, which required only around 100 milliseconds to compute the optimal transport weights on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. All of the underlying source code for our algorithm has been made freely available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/albanGejman/Transport BilinSearch. As proof of its utility, we have successfully applied our algorithm to various real-world scenarios, including a study of the distribution of stars in a galaxy cluster using data from the astrophysics research field. Specifically, we have used our algorithm to compute and visualize the optimal distribution of stars across different sub-clusters in the cluster known as HOX II, which revealed a number of intriguing spatial distribution patterns. Similarly, we have successfully used our algorithm to analyze the cell movement process in a biological experiment. Specifically, we have applied our algorithm to compute a map of the optimal speed for a cell to move between two distributions, which revealed a number of meaningful features. All of the results from these real-world applications are included in the accompanying repository. This mechanism's fundamental properties are as follows. When irradiated, charged particles are accelerated in opposite directions, creating an electric field proportional to their acceleration. This field steers the charged particles of the substance in a specific direction, mimicking Blackett's effect. A study on resistive media has revealed that irradiated materials exhibit an electric field described as the product of the charged particles' acceleration and charge, unaffected by the presence of an external magnetic field. To quantify the phenomenon's strength, a dimensionless parameter based on the ratio of the charged particles' drift velocity to their acceleration has been developed. This parameter has been calculated for both a thin and a thick resistive medium, revealing that the former's contribution to the effect is negligible, whereas the latter's contribution can be significant. A comparison of the effect's strength in various materials has been made using different irradiation energies, while also addressing the effect's stability by measuring the decay time of the induced electric field. Lastly, the effect's potential applications in radiation-driven electricity generation have been explored. This study presents evidence that weakened solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation exhibit a modified version of Lipschitz stability, where the intensity of this modified stability correlates with the size of the solution's initial condition. We also provide specific examples illustrating these modified stability results. Furthermore, we propose that these examples encapsulate a broader principle. Building upon this framework, we suggest a theory that implies the original Hunter-Saxton equation exhibits stability conditioned on the size of its initial condition. While this conditional stability theory is available for a broad class of equations like the CH and KP1, similar methods are not effective in validating conditional Lipschitz stability for the Hunter-Saxton equation. Therefore, the present study relies on novel approaches, including an extension of recent work by the author with J. Roudie which appeared in arXiv:2101.06530. By integrating the ideas from that paper with additional components, we can confirm the modified stability results for weakened solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation. In particular, we use a combination of methods involving fixed points, balance principles, and the author's prior work with M. Li in arXiv:1805.10511. With these approaches, we can extend prior results and achieve modified Lipschitz stability results for weakened solutions of not only the Hunter-Saxton equation but also the surface quasi-geostrophic equation. The study of the surface quasi-geostrophic equation is particularly significant because it is the first instance where we apply the author's recent work with J. Roudie in arXiv:2101.06530 to derive Lipschitz stability results. Using a similar framework, we can obtain more general stability results for a broad class of equations that are similar to the Hunter-Saxton and surface quasi-geostrophic equations. These more general results are available by solving a system of equations for the extended extended KP1 model that was first considered by Shackleton in arXiv:1805.10511. Building upon the ideas from the author's work with M. Li in arXiv:1805.10511, we can derive gain-by-cutoff results for the extended KP1 model. Ultimately, our study allows the derivation of modified Lipschitz stability results and new conditional stability results for a broad class of equations. Based on this principle, a smoothness control algorithm was implemented on a six-degree-of-freedom industrial robot, assessing the impact of various parameters, including auxiliary encoder installation positions, to maximize positioning accuracy and smoothness of the end effector, yielding a 69.7% reduction in oscillatory movements and a 41.1% decrease in the standard deviation of end effector position errors. The results also demonstrate that the combination of two auxiliary encencers provides better results than a single one, offering a promising solution for improving industrial robots' movement quality. To overcome this restriction, the Molecular Continuum concept was introduced, replacing individual atoms with two-dimensional Gaussian fields that mimic their interaction with electrons. We have developed a Multi-Site Quadrature Method that generates finite basis sets of the molecular quadrature type by combining two-dimensional Gaussian fields, thereby enabling the simulation of complex systems that were previously beyond reach due to their size and computational complexity. A newly established link between the MOLCAS quantum chemistry program and our MSC code allows for the efficient generation of the quadrature basis sets from first principles. We have tested our approach by evaluating the electron affinity, ionization energy, and binding energies of simple diatomic molecules with two valence electrons. Our results are in line with the findings of highly accurate full configuration interaction calculations, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness and reliability of our proposed framework. We are confident that our Multi-Site Quadrature Method will play a key role in the further development of the Molecular Continuum concept, thereby enabling the simulation of the entire molecular valley, consisting of hundreds of valence electrons. Furthermore, we are excited about the possibility of extending our approach to more challenging systems, such as proteins, where it could facilitate the simulation of the quasi-persistent electron liquid surrounding their surface. Such groundbreaking developments are now feasible thanks to the substantial reduction in the computational complexity that our proposed framework makes possible. In particular, we have successfully demonstrated the computational efficiency of our MSC code on multi-GPU platforms, thereby enabling the simulation of the quadrature basis sets that contain hundreds of sites with the help of thousands of processing cores. Our proposed reduction in computational complexity and the associated increase in the practical applicability of the Molecular Continuum framework were made possible by the theoretical contributions of the recently established MSC-LIN framework. The MSC-LIN code is a multi-site linear solver that is based on the local quadratic model of its underlying two-dimensional Gaussian field. By effectively addressing the issues of condensation and the related singularity that arises from the exponential decrease in the determinant of the A matrix due to the increase in the size of the molecular quadrature, the MSC-LIN code is now capable of efficiently handling large systems in the linear regime. In particular, we have successfully demonstrated the computational reliability of the MSC-LIN code on multi-GPU platforms, thereby accelerating the linear solving time of the full quadratic model by an order of magnitude. This work formalizes and expands the concept of authority with respect to a directed space, where we consider upper covers as the primary example of authorities. Dually, we examine the concept of a directed finite cover to establish the foundation for a new topology on directed spaces. This topology enables the definition of authorities within this class of spaces. The resulting authority spaces are necessarily finite and have unique properties, including the existence of a basis consisting entirely of finite covers. We introduce an extension to the HOL logic system for expressing formulas based on time, and we demonstrate its use in defining exact definitions of real-valued functions with a temporal element. We also prove key properties of these definitions, including their uniqueness and persistence. Furthermore, we use the definition of a particular function, h, to establish a connection between its argument and a post-processing step in time, and we formally prove its correctness using a well-established logical property. The integration of temporal definitions into HOL is shown through a practical example, which is also made accessible as a runnable HOL theorem within the Coq proof assistant. We ultimately aim to apply these results to establish a link between the languages used for specifying timing constraints in HOL and the fundamental concepts of real-time programming. We provide a major example of how this framework can be employed - a function that generates, on the fly, all possible timing schedules for a given program to ensure its correct real-time execution, thereby allowing for the creation of programs with temporal guarantees, and we demonstrate its specifications and practical implementation in HOL. The successful compilation of HOL into Coq allows for a separate verification of the generated schedules against the program's functional requirements. We also outline a related Coq-based project for automatically checking the timing schedules against the program's low-level machine code using reflection, and we briefly discuss its interface with the Coq-based FIRM compiler for rational formal verification of real-time programs, including a shared use of the scheduler capability. The related Coq project is made accessible via a separate, independent definition that does not affect the HOL logic itself but can be jointly executed and demonstrated with the accompanying Coq code by a single researcher. We estimate that the related Coq project requires approximately 3-4 months of additional development time. The key findings of this work were presented in a pair of papers, one focused on the HOL approach and a second delving into the Coq implementation, presented at the FM 2019 and ICFEM 2019 conferences respectively. Using a computational model that incorporates density functional theory, researchers examined the digital properties of a layer of silicene topped with hexagonal boron nitride substrates. Both molecular and periodic arrangements of the substrates were explored. The results showed that, similar to a silicon carbide heterostructure, the substrates' conduction band edges slope upward and have an inverted band gap orientation relative to an isolated layer of silicene. Notably, the introduction of a single manganese impurity into the silicene layer resulted in the creation of a digital state located within the energy gap. The manganese impurity digital state energy was found to be dependent on the type of substrate used, indicating that these systems have the potential to be utilized in the development of digital materials. Additionally, the manganese impurity digital state was found to be resistant to changes in environment due to its low energy proximity to the substrates' energy gaps. The energy gaps of the manganese impurity digital states were found to be in the range of a few hundred millielectronvolts. The introduction of a gate voltage was also found to be ineffective in modulating the energy of the manganese impurity digital states. However, the energy gaps of the manganese impurity digital states were found to be sensitive to changes in spin orientation, which can be modulated either electrostatically or through the application of molecular doping. The manganese impurity digital states were found to have the potential to store data as well as act as quantum bits in the development of quantum computing systems. The distinctive electronic properties of Mn-adorned silicene were found to be rooted in the breaking of spatial symmetry in combination with the presence of a hexagonal boron nitride substrate. The theoretical model results were validated through the analysis of the finite size of van Hove singularities in the density of states. A new concept in the development of digital materials has thus been identified - the concept of substrate-induced digital states. The goal of text categorization is to assign one or more labels to an unseen document based on a predefined set of categories. Because many documents can belong to multiple categories, over-sampling in categorization is critical to maintain statistical balance in the dataset. We examined three techniques for creating replicas of the under-represented classes in the document dataset: random oversampling, over-sampling using SMOTE (Simple Simulated Oversampling Technique), and a modified version of SMOTE incorporating Pearson's correlation. We evaluated these methods through experiments using six datasets from the knowledge discovery and information extraction domain, comparing accuracy and F-measure values. Accuracies and F-measure values for single and multiple-class problems were calculated using different evaluation metrics, and a statistical significance test was conducted to analyze the results. We found that incorporating oversampling improved accuracy and F-measure values but the most effective method varied depending on the dataset. While the modified SMOTE technique performed well for single-class problems, its performance was inconsistent for multiple-class problems. Random oversampling and using SMOTE on the majority class yielded better results for different datasets. Hence, the choice of oversampling method relies on the dataset and leads to improved performance but not in all cases. Therefore, the presence of oversampling methods when building categorizers is not a straightforward issue. Knowledge of the dataset's influence on the choice of oversampling method is essential and this paper aims to contribute towards gaining such knowledge. In addition to improving accuracy and F-measure values, the other crucial issue in categorization is the threshold value for confidence and this paper aims to contribute towards gaining such knowledge as well. We investigated three threshold values, 0.51, 0.76 and 0.95 for F-measure values and accuracy metrics for different classes and found some trade-offs in the threshold values and the classification metrics. Therefore, the choice of threshold value depends on whether one wants to improve the accuracy or the F-measure values and this paper aims to contribute towards gaining such knowledge. Knowledge of the threshold value and its influence on the classification metrics is essential and this paper aims to contribute towards gaining such knowledge. In addition to the F-measure value of an individual class, the other crucial issue in categorization is the recognition of the classes among the top ranks. We collected data from 177 stations, including 124 ABC, 67 CBS, and 46 FOX, and created an index of their coverage, based on the frequency and tone of news content, from January to May 2020. We then examined the connections between this information and COVID cases and deaths in each region, as well as the reaction of the local audiences. We also discovered significant correlations between the index and COVID deaths, but not when considering the total number of cases. Our research suggests that local TV stations' coverage had a notable effect on the pandemic's outcome, which might be attributed to various factors such as the stations' influence on public opinion and the behavior of their viewers. We also provide a framework for investigating the potential consequences of a news source's tone and tone variations, such as a conservative or liberal orientation. Our model consists of four variables: the number of cases or deaths, a source's index of coverage, a region's characteristics, and a control variable representing cases or deaths. We recommend applying this framework to various contexts beyond our COVID-19 study. A significant implication of our findings is that the tone of local news, which is often shaped by the ownership of the stations, can have a substantial impact on the outcome of a public health crisis like the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study provides initial evidence of this connection, which warrants further exploration. We provide a detailed overview of the pandemic's consequences in the United States, including the overall trend and the state-by-state outcomes. We also report on the characteristics of the regions, such as divided opinions among local audiences, a greater spread in COVID cases or deaths, and a higher mortality rate in counties where CBS news was given more attention, as opposed to a more uniform outcome in ABC and FOX cases. Our investigation is conducted as a multi-disciplinary research that combines computational methods to create an index of coverage for each local TV station, gather regional data, and analyze it as a Bayesian network model. The Rapid Multipole Method, a computationally efficient algorithm that acceleres N-body simulations by exploiting the hierarchy of frequencies, is based on a key assumption that higher-order multipoles do not substantially affect the motion of outer system bodies. While this assumption is well-understood in terms of energy, its implications for angular momentum are more nuanced and have been the subject of speculation. We have now rigorously examined the preservation of angular momentum in RM simulations, starting with a detailed analysis of Hamiltonian mapping and extending to higher-order Taylor expansions. Our results suggest that, unless specific precautions are taken, the integration of RM is inherently non-conserving under both Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks, leading to a gradual decline in angular momentum with time. This finding is in line with previous observations of an apparent conservation of angular momentum in certain RM realizations. We have successfully modified the standard Eulerian integration scheme to ensure that higher-order multipoles do not affect the angular momentum, and numerical simulations have confirmed that this adapted method preserves angular momentum with high accuracy. Importantly, our research demonstrates that the angular momentum conservation, a fundamental property of N-body systems, can be restored in RM simulations, and that our adapted method does not compromise the energy conservation, thus maintaining O(N) computational complexity. Our team has conducted a series of simulations to verify these outcomes through multiple test cases. Our paper provides a detailed mathematical explanation of these accomplishments and supports our findings with a comprehensive suite of numerical simulations in various N-body scenarios. These results are expected to significantly benefit the N-body and NFT community by empowering researchers to achieve both efficient and accurate simulations. Our new integration algorithm, preserving both energy and angular momentum, maintains the same computational complexity as the standard RM method and is publicly available at https://github.com/alexeyerke/RapidMultipoleMethod. We have also made demographic information available for distribution via https://github.com/alexeyerke/RapidMultipoleMethod/blob/main/adaptive_step_size.md. The associated repository contains our code, which we have thoroughly documented to facilitate future development and use. Our numerical experiments, displayed in Figure 49 through Figure 50, illustrate the key contributions of our study, and their data is publicly available from the above repository. The code used in our context, primarily written in Julia, can be accessed at https://github.com/alexeyerke/RapidMultipoleMethod. To facilitate the review and identification of potential biases, our numerical results are presented in a standard format, and our code, thoroughly documented, can be easily replicated.

There are many situations where trained models are available but cannot be directly accessed due to issues such as copyright, privacy concerns, or the high computational costs of training large models, representing an "inaccessible expert". The term "data amplification" refers to the process of utilizing a limited number of samples from a difficult-to-access expert to improve a model trained only on a rich but disorganized sampling environment. The concept of data amplification has been explored in the context of reinforcement learning using rich sampling environments. However, the effectiveness of this process relies on the rich sampling environment being similar to the target environment, a requirement not necessarily met in the case of high-stakes applications such as medical procedures, where different patient cases may not be similar. The existing methods work poorly when the rich sampling environment does not accurately represent the target domain, resulting in the transfer of irrelevant knowledge. To resolve this issue, a new method of data amplification in the context of reinforcement learning has been developed to effectively learn from inaccessible experts by utilizing a combined approach of transferring knowledge and eliminating irrelevant behavior. The proposed algorithm has been tested using a variety of simulations and a real-world medical procedure application, demonstrating its superiority over the previous state-of-the-art method. The source code for this project has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/andreab Rossi/data_amplification.git.
