A comprehensive study of the creation and detection of pairs of Higgs bosons generated in conjunction with a vector boson has been conducted. Utilizing 36.1 fb^-1 of data collected by the ATLAS detector in 2015-2016 from high-energy proton collisions at 13 TeV, researchers examined Higgs pairs formed through the weak interaction between two similar fundamental particles. By analyzing the characteristics of these Higgs bosons as detected via up to six jets, up to two leptons, and up to eight leptons, a distinct signal was sought. If a specific Higgs production mechanism is absent, the probability of detecting this signal was also determined for certain types of events. As no significant difference from expected interactions was found, this research established new, sensitive lower limits on the production of Higgs pairs in association with vector bosons. Specifically, this research considered possible interactions between Higgs bosons and vector bosons such as Z bosons, W bosons, and photons at 95% confidence levels. For example, this research determined that for Higgs bosons interacting via the weak interaction, the possible mass ranges for Higgs pairs were below 1.35 TeV; for Higgs bosons interacting via the Yukawa interaction between similar fundamental particles, the possible mass ranges were below 1.20 TeV; and for Higgs bosons interacting via the Yukawa interaction between fundamental particles of different types, the possible mass ranges were below 1.58 TeV. These new lower limits represent an improvement of 20-40% over previously measured lower limits, which were conducted in 2017. Furthermore, this research considered possible interactions between Higgs bosons and gravitons. For gravitons, the possible interactions between Higgs bosons and fundamental particles of gravity were not found, which establishes a new, sensitive lower limit on the production of gravitons for the first time. Laser technology has significantly impacted daily life and scientific progress. Although the development of spin lasers is still in its early stages, they have the potential to contribute substantially to the advancement of technical optics. A distinct characteristic of spin lasers is that the population inversion is achieved through the angular momentum of particles rather than their linear momentum. This unique feature might offer a more robust framework for understanding electromagnetic interactions. In this context, we present a model of an electronic alkali spin laser, which employs a ring cavity containing alkali metals like rubidium or cesium. The cavity is surrounded by a superconducting coil producing a strong magnetic field that freezes the electron spin and forces the laser to operate in a single transverse mode. Although this concept has its limitations, it provides a novel approach for investigating the interaction between spin angular and orbital momenta in atoms, as well as a method for creating highly coherent and polarized spin waves in the optical and magnetic domain. Furthermore, the method demonstrates the possibility of generating coherent spin waves in magnetic materials by employing a magnetic field instead of a laser field. The model also showcases a new technique for creating highly coherent and polarized spin waves in the magnetic domain. The idea of using a superconducting coil to create a spin laser is also proposed as a potential solution to the challenge of achieving a population inversion without cooling the system. The potential applications of this concept in research on spin angular momentum, the interaction between matter and electromagnetic fields, and in the development of highly coherent and polarized spin waves, mean that electronic spin lasers could play a significant role in the advancement of technical optics and in experiments in the field of technical optics. The model presented here is based on the principles of optical angular momentum, which links the spin angular momentum of the laser field to its orbital angular momentum. In this context, the spin angular momentum of the laser field is achieved not through a population inversion but through the freezing of the electron spin under a strong external magnetic field. The concept of using a superconducting coil to create a population inversion without cooling the system in spin lasers is innovative and could potentially be applied in the development of highly coherent and polarized spin waves in the optical and magnetic domain. The model also demonstrates the possibility of creating spin waves in the magnetic domain by applying a magnetic field to the system instead of a laser field. The potential applications of this concept in the development of technical optics and in experiments in the field could be substantial. This paper proposes a novel distributed optimization algorithm, the Distributed Active Convex Conjugate Gradient (DACCG), which tackles the challenge of minimizing the average of $N$ individual functions across multiple agents, without requiring them to be accessible in advance. Each agent applies an active set method (a specific variant of conjugate gradient) to its assigned function and shares gradient updates with neighboring agents, facilitating coordinated optimization. As the number of active variables in each function grows, the algorithm's efficiency is similar to state-of-the-art distributed first-order methods. Even when the number of active variables is limited, DACCG offers enhanced performance over existing techniques. This is achieved using a customized potential function, allowing the algorithm's convergence rates to be quantified. Experimental results demonstrate that DACCG operates efficiently across various problem scenarios and multiple scales of active variables without relying on extensive tuning of parameters. Furthermore, its execution costs are comparable to that of broadcast-based methods, with scalable communication overhead. Additionally, DACCG's memory utilization is kept minimal with each agent holding only $O(\sqrt{k})$ variables at any given time, where $k$ represents the number of active variables in each function. This is accomplished by periodically adjusting the active set, resulting in substantial storage savings when dealing with sparse functions. As a result, DACCG presents a highly efficient and adaptable solution for distributed optimization tasks. Its distributed and resource-efficient nature makes it suitable for large-scale cooperative machine learning applications. As robots increasingly share tasks with humans, conveying intentions and goals becomes a critical safety issue. To prevent collisions while sharing spaces with humans, autonomous robots must be able to communicate their purposes clearly. In the realm of shared autonomy, particularly in environments with dense traffic, like cities or airports, understanding a robot's intentions in real-time is crucial for avoiding accidents. We developed a new system of visual symbols and associated recognition technology to help Conveying Robots, designed to carry loads, communicate their objectives to humans. Our system implies goals through visual connections between the robot and its load, and we have created a user-friendly interface to input these intentions via a handheld device. Experiments involving actual goal statements from a load and perceptions from human observers have demonstrated high levels of understanding for our intended communication strategy. Additionally, goal-related questions from a human participant failed to significantly impact the understanding of the shared autonomy system used in our trial. In environments with video footage of a robot and load, our technology has also effectively identified the robot's intended communication based on the information provided. In a complex environment resembling a busy city, our technology has successfully predicted that a robot's visual symbols would lead humans to understand the robot's desired path, and we have seen corresponding adjustments in human behavior as a result. In line with previous research on the shared autonomy system, our trial has shown that, during joint tasks, shared autonomy systems lead to predictable and stable interactions, and these interactions become part of a shared understanding. In conclusion, our technology has effectively communicated the Conveying Robot's intentions to both visually observe the robot and interact with it directly. We investigate how electron scattering and propagation around corners, as well as the immersing medium, influence the gap plasmons that occur in the narrow gaps of hybridized nanostructures composed of lattices of conductive and insulating materials. Our analysis considers both the surface and interface plasmons that emerge in the interfacial regions and the narrow gaps of the structure. The surface plasmons that arise at the external surfaces of the conductive regions remain unaffected by the changes in the narrow gaps, in contrast to the interface and gap plasmons that form at the interfaces and within the gaps of the structure, which are highly responsive to the changes in the interfacial areas and frequencies. Our analysis predicts that as the interfacial areas decrease, the gap plasmons that are associated with them will shift to lower frequencies and become less damped. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in leveraging context for deep learning models to enhance NLP tasks such as part-of-speech tagging and neural machine translation.  Additionally, research has been conducted to develop a contextual understanding for knowledge acquisition, particularly in the domain of named entity extraction (EE), given its vital role in constructing semantic knowledge graphs, a crucial component for multiple down-stream applications.  While numerous NEE approaches have been explored, they often suffer from data inefficiency as they disregard the contextual dependencies within the training data and treat each sample independently.  To address this limitation, we introduce Term Significance Feedback (TSF) to aid multiple contextual deep learning models, including BERT, to accurately acquire new names and enhance entity classification during the training process.  Our experiments on Wikipedia and NELL datasets demonstrate that TSF surpasses traditional benchmark performance by at least 2% and also outperforms current contextual state-of-the-art methods while further leveraging their capabilities.  Our comprehensive evaluation and analytical examination of TSF performance indicate that it surpasses existing approaches by incorporating contextual understanding through enhanced feature extraction, name representation, and name-related memory formation. A cost-effective approach to adjusting these models involves "adapter modules" that can be easily trained and adapted to various tasks within the same model. As a result, the UTA can be trained more quickly while achieving better performance compared to other methods.  When integrated with other training strategies like knowledge distillation and gradient elastic averaging, the UTA can significantly improve the performance and efficiency of adapter-based large language models. When considering a set of items, people often have preferences about which items to add, taking into account what is already in the set. The study of such preferences can be modeled through information gap theory, particularly when evaluating the addition of sets. A survey revealed a significant difference in people's risk preferences in the context-based model, but not when their preferences were expressed numerically and evaluated in a non-contextual manner. The results show that people tend to be more averse to risk when their preferences are considered in a non-contextual manner, but this aversion decreases when their preferences are considered in a context-dependent manner. The study's results are consistent with the theory of loss aversion and provide implications for the addition of sets, highlighting the importance of considering the interdependence of people's preferences. By employing a specific protocol, we measure the entropy production rate and assess the validity of the geometric inequality in these glass-forming liquids. We find that the interior of the compact beta cluster, which develops from a local rearrangement in the alpha liquid, influences the entropy production rate. This local compact structure drives the alpha to beta transition in the liquid, supported by observations that the geometric inequality is satisfied throughout the transition, with the liquid in a metastable state prior to this local compact structure forming. This finding implies that the alpha to beta transition in polymer liquids is a multi-step process involving changes in dynamics without changes in the entropy production rate or configurational entropy. Following the initial local compact structure formation, which slows down dynamics, the liquid undergoes rapid cluster growth. This rapid growth phase, which contributes to the geometric inequality not being satisfied, eventually leads to structural saturation and stable equilibrium in the liquid. This rapid growth phase was previously mistaken for the native beta structure in polymer liquids, which is a misconception that has been in error. In contrast to the geometric inequality not being satisfied during the rapid growth phase, we find that it is satisfied during the slow growth phase, which involves growing clusters in systems that are equilibrium or near-equilibrium. This finding implies that the slow growth phase, which involves growing clusters in equilibrium or near-equilibrium conditions, may be the natural path to forming extra-stable glassy structures in polymer liquids. This potential route to forming extra-stable glassy structures in polymer liquids could be explored through molecular engineering that involves creating native structures in equilibrium or near-equilibrium conditions, which requires a specific geometric relationship to be satisfied. This application has potential to advance our understanding in the field of glass formation in polymer liquids. To improve translation quality, especially when dealing with rare or
unseen terms during real-time translation, a critical challenge needs to be addressed. The existing production models in neural machine translation (NMT) look back at past production history, which hinders their ability to handle rare or unseen terms. The proposed module, called the look-forward attention (LFA) module, utilizes context from the produced so far and the alignment between the source and target languages to guide the translation process. By incorporating this module into production models, the translation process is informed not only by the past production history but also by the alignment between the source and target languages. The LFA module has been implemented in three forms: an unsupervised version with no additional training objectives, a supervised version, and a semi-supervised version that does not require extra training objectives. The experimental results show that the LFA module enhances the translation quality when integrated with the chen2018look production model. The implementation details and the trained models will be made publicly available. Moreover, a new production model that combines the LFA module and the chen2018look production model has been proposed to overcome the limitation of looking back at past production history. The production model, called the LFA-proposal model, maintains a balanced approach by using the unsupervised LFA module to propose alignments and a controlled version of the proposal mechanism to select relevant proposals based on the alignment weights. To evaluate the effectiveness of the LFA module and the LFA-proposal model, both have been implemented on two production models: the chen2018look model and the gu-2018 neural production model. The experimental results show that the LFA-proposal model outperforms the baseline production models by a large margin. The implementation details and the trained models will be made publicly available. The research finds that the LFA-proposal model's translation quality improvements can be attributed to two key factors: its ability to accurately propose alignments and to control the proposal mechanism to ensure that only relevant alignments are considered. As a result, the LFA-proposal model achieves significant translation quality gains that continue to improve over time. The research's findings highlight the importance of looking forward to improve translation quality, especially when dealing with rare or unseen terms during real-time translation. To address this, various numerical solutions have been developed, although lacking a consensus on the conservation of key properties like total density and energy. To overcome this issue, we have constructed a novel conservative Galerkin solver for the quasilinear Fokker-Planck equation, along with a flexible finite-element method implementation. Our approach, with its extensive flux correction method based on the cumulative error distribution, allows for an accurate solution of the quasilinear equation while ensuring the preservation of plasma density and energy. Notably, we have demonstrated our model's capabilities through applications to both a simplified wave-resonant plasma and a more complex stellarator, providing valuable insights into the behavior of magnetized plasmas. Furthermore, our model has the flexibility to extend to additional physical processes like turbulent fluctuations and their effects on wave-particle interactions. As such, we believe that our model has the potential to improve our understanding of complex plasma dynamics and to facilitate the development of improved plasma control systems. This study presents a theoretical assessment of the direct and parasitic beam-induced background impacts on signal measurements in muon colliders. Specifically, we examine the background generated by full-intensity muon beams, damping rings, and muon injection/extracted systems. We also investigate the effectiveness of various beam manipulation strategies for reducing this background. Notably, we conclude that by employing a 'anti-signal' beam, it is possible to eliminate direct background signals. This achievement, however, relies on the approximate cancellation of induced background muons at the collision point. In cases where this cancellation isn't possible, the reduced direct background signal comes at the cost of increased parasitic background signals. This fact underlines the importance of a sophisticated beam delivery system design for achieving high signal precision in muon colliders. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that utilizing a low-charge anti-signal beam with low longitudinal density can significantly reduce (potentially by an order of magnitude) the required precision in horizontal beam profile for achieving desired collider levels, to $0.78\,\mathrm{mm}$. This improvement translates to lower technical requirements for the beam delivery system and the collider itself. Ultimately, we conclude that our proposed beam reduction technique can greatly contribute to reaching our goal of attaining a background limited by detector sensitivity at next-generation muon colliders. We have initiated initial discussions with the FCCee collaboration about integrating our strategy into their design process. By applying a suitable extension of the characteristic method, we've established the existence of characteristics for such processes. Our results also demonstrate that as the time step reduces, the solution of a discrete process will converge to the solution of a continuous, nonlinear differential process, even when the convergence criteria are rather lax. To achieve this, we've first defined what constitutes a moving convex-sweeping process in a functional framework, and have established key properties for such processes in relation to a suitable extension of the difference quotient. Moreover, our paper illustrates the practical utility of these results through two case studies, involving nonlinear vibration problems with obstacles that are moving at a varying pace. These cases demonstrate the importance of considering nonlinearity when analyzing such problems, as well as the need to examine the sweeping process in the context of its starting point, especially when certain conditions are not met. Moreover, our paper includes numerical examples to fortify its analytical findings, showcasing the difficulties that can arise in such problems, and how these difficulties are addressed through the characteristic method. We focus on developing a technique, known as reverse reinforcement learning (RRL), which enables us to establish a model that mimics a robot's task-based learning system.  Our model is grounded in economic principles and is built around the concept of a chief executive officer (CEO) who sets a series of reward parameters in order to maximize the overall profit generated by a robot.  In return, the robot learns to optimize its control policies in accordance with the CEO's decisions in the form of pre-defined Q-function values.  One of the main advantages of our approach is its ability to model a team of robots, as well as to adapt to changing reward schemes.  In our research, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by evaluating it using a complex robotic task - the cooperation required to move bulky objects through an environment that is heavily influenced by gravity.  In doing so, we are also able to effectively model and manipulate the behaviors that emerge from this scenario.  Furthermore, we explore the scenario in which the robot's policies are not provided as input, but instead, we train the RRL model using a collection of trial-and-error data.  Our numerical results demonstrate that it is possible for the RRL model to generate a wide range of tasks and policies that are similar to those that are created through traditional reward tuning.  One of the key benefits of our approach is its ability to separate the process of task definition from policy execution, thus yielding several important applications such as automatic policy validation, as well as the creation of a library of pre-designed policies.  Our paper delves into these applications and outlines the various implications that our research has from both theoretical and practical perspectives.  Additionally, we also demonstrate that our approach can be effective in modeling the behaviors of self-interested robots in a cooperative environment by using an internal representation of the CEO's incentives in conjunction with the observation of the robot's actions.  Our numerical results verify that the proposed method is capable of modeling a wide range of RRL tasks in a cooperative environment. Quantifying uncertainties in physics-innovated neural networks is crucial for issues like predicting the life of aircraft components and understanding cancer progression. Present methods for evaluating uncertainty primarily apply to datasets obtained directly from measurements, but not modified datasets generated through inverse problems. We introduce a novel approach to uncertainty quantification for physics-innovated neural networks, which utilizes a network designed for posterior error estimation. This approach utilizes two relatively simple neural networks to accurately predict the probability distribution of potential errors in problems with ordinary differential equations and can be modified to include partial differential equations with minimal additional complexity. We successfully test this method in problems involving oscillating functions, implicit differential equations, and partial differential equations representing both steady and dynamic conditions. Our results show that the estimated and true error distributions closely align, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach. Further details on the implementation and validation of this method are available in a publicly accessible repository. This work has been successfully applied to a specific problem in the field of authorized machine learning during an experiment at the Brookhaven National Laboratory. Specifically, it was used to analyze data related to ion beam analysis with uncertain detector readings. This method enables generating reliable uncertainty quantification for such sensor detectors without employing calibration procedures or measuring calibration data. We believe this approach can be adapted and successfully applied to a broad range of issues within authorized machine learning. Furthermore, it has the potential to be integrated into an automatic processing system for automatically processing and fine-tuning the parameters of neural networks in automated workflows. When completely automated, this method could lead to significant and timely improvements in the uncertainty quantification for neural networks in authorized machine learning during 24/7 operations. Additionally, this technique could be integrated into other AI systems for even greater automation and efficiency. Deep learning with Graph Convolutional Networks has achieved significant success in data analysis, but the reliance on assumption of noise-free data is a major limitation. In real-world applications, data contamination is a pervasive issue that often goes undetected during training. Reinforcement learning has shown its limitations in learning intractable probability distributions, especially when the data is annotated with reliability metrics. This research introduces a reinforcement learning strategy to mitigate contamination in GNNs by leveraging reliable training data. We propose a new algorithm, the Robust Graph Reinforcement Trainer (GROR), that utilizes a dynamic selection of contamination-free training samples to maximize its return. Our findings demonstrate that GROR can effectively counteract contamination in GNNs with various noise models on both synthetic and real-world datasets, improving accuracy compared to traditional loss functions. This is particularly evident in scenarios with severe contamination where conventional loss functions fail to produce results. GROR's effectiveness also extends to situations where the data has no annotations, and we provide a detailed analysis of its adaptations for such applications. Domain-specific knowledge capture systems such as information ontologies systematically gather facts linking core concepts to more specific ideas within a particular domain. As these systems grow, managing and maintaining their extensive knowledge becomes challenging. To address this issue, this research introduces OntoPlot, a visualization tool that displays relationships between concepts in an ontology in an interactive, circular layout. The purpose of such a visualization is to enable users to discover new connections between concepts, understand hierarchies, and clarify core concept classifications. To assess OntoPlot's effectiveness, this study conducts usability tests and compares its performance with existing visualizations using Bioontology knowledge base, MeSH. The evaluation includes an expert user study and various quantitative studies that compare OntoPlot's performance across different scales. The results indicate that, overall, OntoPlot outperforms traditional hierarchical visualizations like tree maps and space tree, providing enhanced insights and efficiency when navigating and understanding large ontologies composed of up to 8 levels of core concepts. Notably, OntoPlot's performance benefits significantly due to the relatively small number of core concepts in existing ontologies, making it a valuable visualization tool for data engineers working with large graph databases in various domains. The future potential integration of interactive query mechanisms, such as those found in database visualizations, further solidifies OntoPlot's status as a useful tool for data exploration and understanding. The development of OntoPlot has been guided by the principles of user-centered design. A prototype of the OntoPlot has been developed using the CTool library, allowing users to interactively navigate and understand ontologies. Importantly, OntoPlot's performance compares favorably to existing solutions, providing visualizations for up to 350,000 nodes in a circle and 700,000 nodes in a linear layout. We recently made significant improvements to an end-to-end automatic speech recognition system by exploiting a previously underutilized set of unlabelled data. We applied a innovative approach that combines an end-to-end model with a discriminator from a different domain, and implemented cycle-consistency to train the model in an inter-domain context. This approach not only rewarded accurate transcription but also the speaker who produced the utterance, leading to a faster model-speed trade-off. As a result, our method exhibited a substantial gain in speech recognition accuracy, with a 9% decrease in word error rate when using a 1GB model compared to a smaller 350MB variant. This breakthrough enables the creation of highly accurate and compact ASR models, paving the way for integrated speech and language processing on mobile devices and mobile computing systems using specialized hardware. We also showcased the potential for our technique to enhance other related tasks, such as speech synthesis, by transforming utterances into novel languages, and demonstrating its promise in a speech translation task from English to Hindi. We also tested our method in a number of other languages and made the source code available online. Our results demonstrate that with a large set of unlabelled data and our novel inter-domain approach, an end-to-end ASR system can significantly surpass the performance of earlier classifier-based models. Our findings stress the importance of considering domain influence in the design of ASR systems and the potential for future advancements by leveraging data from different domains to improve system performance. A key challenge in independent robot navigation involves determining the optimal movement sequence to achieve desired goals, given limited information about the environment. Our approach tackles this issue by assuming that the robot's world is comprised of a network of nodes representing state goals, and that each node is linked to a set of adjacent states. To effectively navigate, the robot needs to identify the most efficient path between the current state and the desired goal state, and then move to the next state along this path. To address this problem, we utilize a predictive model based on Deep Active Inference, consisting of two interconnected layers of interacting neural systems. The model's generative model layer generates the next state of the system in response to an internal drive and the current state, while the active model layer determines the next state to which the robot should be driven to maximize the likelihood of reaching the goal state. To model uncertainty in the environment, we incorporate variational inference and a learned environment graph that is adjusted at each time step, based on the current state. Our method outperformed traditional algorithms in controlled simulations, and demonstrated robustness to noise and unpredictable interruptions. It successfully achieved goal-oriented exploration and adaptation in complex environments characterized by diverse dynamics, as shown in a game requiring goal-seeking and adaptation. Our work contributes a novel Deep Active Inference framework for tackling key challenges in independent robot navigation. It also validates the potential of Predictive Brain Models in addressing fundamental issues in artificial intelligence and related applications. To incorporate syntax into neural machine translation and parsing models, a new decoding approach is suggested, which builds upon a neural dependency parsing model developed by Koutnik et al. (2017). This method allows for the utilization of syntax to direct translation and parsing generation. Initially, a syntax-directed translation and parsing model is formulated by combining a neural machine translation model with a syntactic linking model, which predicts the syntax tree and link annotations from a given source sentence. Then, to obtain syntax-linked representations, the model proceeds to predict not only word by word translations, but also tree structure and syntactic links simultaneously during decoding. This results in a model that uses a syntax-ased decoding method to predict target sentences. Experimental outcomes on the English-to-German and English-to-Russian datasets from the WMT2019 Neural Machine Translation Shared Task demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method. Furthermore, model integration with n-best lists leads to notable improvements in translation quality, which amounts to a 1.2 and 1.0 BLEU points increase in English-to-German and English-to-Russian respectively when compared with the baseline model. Additionally, model integration with the state-of-the-art stack-based dependency parsing model yields consistent gains in parsing accuracy on the CoNLL-2015 dataset, amounting to a 1.2 percentage point improvement. This new top-down decoding method also opens new avenues for model design, such as the use of bottom-up models and pretraining techniques. This provides an additional avenue for potential improvement and development in this area. Finally, the model's top-down decoding process is not only limited to neural machine translation and dependency parsing but can also be applied to any model with a graph structure, which makes it a highly versatile method. This kind of decoding process allows for the exploration of new ideas in natural language processing tasks that also involve graph-based decoding. A new database, the Binding Energy Assessment Platform, has been created to provide computational researchers with a comprehensive set of intermolecular binding energies for diverse astrophysical species. This database sets out to fill the gap in a widely-used binding energy dataset, which excluded key astrophysical species due to the constraints of the underlying quantum chemical calculations. To overcome these limitations, the Binding Energy Assessment Platform uses a statistical analysis approach that compares experimentally-verified binding energies to a set of theoretical estimates, known as binding energy distributions. This flexible platform allows for the easy addition of new species and the assessment of their binding energies, all while adhering to strict scientific standards. To illustrate the capabilities of the platform, the database provides binding energies for nine diverse astrophysical species, which can be used in future studies to assess and refine the accuracy of astrophysical chemical reaction rates. This assessment will in turn aid in a deeper understanding of the complex chemical reactions occurring in space, which are crucial for creating a more accurate model of astrochemical binding. Ultimately, the Binding Energy Assessment Platform serves as a valuable resource for the astrochemical community, empowering researchers to make data-driven decisions in pursuit of breakthroughs in the field of astrochemistry. This study was conducted for the NASA Astrobiology Institute's Deciphering Solars and Exoplanetary Volatiles (DEVOL) research program, with the support of the UNLV's Solar System and Earths: Astrophysical and Geological Climate Modeling Center for the study of modern and ancient Earths and other planets. To the knowledge of the authors, no similar benchmarking databases exist for the evaluation of quantum mechanical and reaction kinetics simulation models, which the BEAP could potentially be expanded to include in the future. A related GitHub repository can be found at https://github.com/UNLV-ASTR/BEAP. Further information on the BEAP can be accessed at the website (https://beap.astro.unlv.edu/). A tutorial on how to use the BEAP is available at http://www.astro.unlv.edu/tutor/unlv0000/BEAP.htm. The 9 species included in the initial release have been chosen for their significant astrochemical relevance, with more to be added in the near future by request. The initial phase of machine learning involves recognizing basic patterns. Despite a lack of universal understanding about the nature of these patterns from the user's perspective, we investigate a specific case where the user outlines the desired pattern using a few selected data points. By formulating this problem as a learning challenge across different domains, we examine methods to adapt to new patterns encountered during training. Furthermore, we develop a method to establish whether a particular learning method is effective across multiple domains by using the principle of minimality. In this context, we demonstrate that the Bayesian learning approach is the simplest and most effective method to adapt to new patterns and establish generalization across different domains. This method requires no pre-processing of the patterns or hyper-parameter adjustments when transferring between domains. It is even feasible for the user to dynamically change the defined data points or the learning objectives in real-time without needing to modify the underlying code. We provide theoretical justification for these claims and showcase our approach through a series of practical examples. In addition to theoretical discussion, we also compare our approach with other established learning methods. Moreover, we outline the future research possibilities in this area, including the possibility of creating an intelligent interface to facilitate the user's interaction with the learning algorithm and displaying the learned pattern in an intuitive manner. The quantization approach is implemented using the Binary Cross-Kinny Center (BCKC) method, while the word extraction method utilizes neural network-based signs for determining vector distribution patterns in training data. The performance of the two techniques is evaluated and compared, with promising results showing that both methods can successfully reduce the impact of language id variations on performance, thereby enabling the benefits of multilingual data to be harnessed to improve low-resource mt translation accuracy and reduce the word error rate. The measurement uncertainty principle poses a fundamental question about whether a single measurement can reveal two mutually exclusive properties of an object. Quantum theory indicates that, upon a measurement, a system $S$ must definitely either exhibit property $A$ or property $B$, yet this does not necessarily mean that $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive properties. However, since this is indeed the common understanding, many scientists accept this without question as fact. This paper argues that this widespread assumption is unwarranted and results in unnecessary limitations to quantum theory. Furthermore, we propose a new model based on the principle of state duplication and suggest that property exclusivity should be treated as a condition that arises from the distinct processes of state duplication corresponding to each property. This idea is formulated as a variational problem with meaningful applications. The main goal of this paper is to explain the quantum distinguishability issue and its underlying physics, rather than presenting a formal theory. As such, we do not aim to provide a comprehensive and mathematical definition of the key concepts involved. Rather, our goal is to present a conceptual model that highlights the primary physical characteristics, with the accompanying mathematics serving as a descriptive tool. Finally, we speculate on the potential implications of this new understanding of quantum theory and suggest areas for further exploration. Specifically, we aim to investigate its connections to the theories of quantum complementarity and quantum indistinguishability. The main ideas presented in this paper are as follows. (1) The measurement uncertainty principle should be reinterpreted as a distinguishability problem. (2) The concept of state duplication should be central to this interpretation. (3) Property distinguishability should be treated as a variational problem. (4) The global unitary evolution operator should be used to model the duplication process corresponding to a property. (5) The re-interpretation in idea (1) has significant and non-trivial consequences when extended to the context of quantum channels, thereby providing new insights into the realm of quantum non-locality. (6) The connections between the proposed model and existing concepts such as quantum complementarity, quantum indistinguishability, and coherence preservation should be explored. (7) The model's potential implications for the development of quantum advantage should be identified. (8) The model's limitations and potential areas for further refinement should also be examined.

This work focuses on a specific action by Aurillo et al., analogous to the Hilbert-Einstein action, but formulated within double field theory. By examining the theory's Lagrangian and Maxwell equations, we demonstrate that they can be expressed in terms of the Lee-Wey-Tzeng action, a form invariant under volume transformations. We establish that the theory's action and electromagnetic propagation are influenced by a novel curvature scalar, proportional to the $H_{ij}$ component of the Ricci tensor. This discovery enables us to devise a unified framework for testing these theories, incorporating standard tests such as perihelion shifts and BSSN equations, as well as new tests based on bending angles, Zeldovich potentials, and Newcomb's surfaces. By identifying the break-down scale $\Lambda$ of these theories, we show that the theories become equivalent to general relativity at distances greater than the Planck scale. Future experiments near solar objects can probe these theories by using a combination of general, novel, and ongoing consistency tests. Additionally, we plan to integrate these theories with quantum gravity in the near and far future, aiming to identify a specific action by testing a novel, non-Riemannian invariant during near-future experiments at the LISA facility. Such a breakthrough could fundamentally alter our understanding of gravity and cosmic evolution, challenging existing concepts and opening up fresh avenues of research. A related computational tool, called gravity, has been developed for testing these theories and made freely available to the research community. This software enables the efficient simulation of gravitational fields, electromagnetic propagation, and related effects, as well as the automatic derivation of Maxwell equations and Lagrangian. By utilizing this tool and our testing framework, we plan to facilitate the comparison of existing implementations and new models within the gravitational physics community. One of the key features of this software is its ability to inherit existing accuracy from general relativity while introducing novel effects, even if the new action can be expressed in terms of the Lee-Wey-Tzeng form. To meet growing demands for Internet access, service providers are increasing the density of WiFi access points in residential areas, which often results in a coexistence problem among their network devices. Since customers choose their own WiFi equipment, providers face a challenge in managing these access points, which makes it difficult for them to control the network and deliver quality services. To address this issue, we suggest a new strategy where customers are provided with leased WiFi access points or extenders, and these devices report channel information to the provider, enabling it to optimize its network by selecting the most suitable equipment for each location. By doing so, the provider can eliminate performance problems in its network. To manage the channel information of all possible locations, only selected nodes, chosen based on the topology of the provider's network, need to report their information, which minimizes the load on the provider's management system. By testing our proposal in a large-scale experiment, we found that our solution can effectively mitigate performance degradation and maintain stability in crowded WiFi networks, while also saving energy by optimizing the choice of WiFi equipment for each location. To implement our proposal, we only need to modify the channel information request function in the IEEE 802.11k/v standard, which makes our solution compatible with both providers and customers. Our experiment, which evaluated our proposal with Intel's dual-band WiFi adapter, showed that its ability to choose the optimal WiFi equipment successfully exceeded its target value of 80%. Furthermore, by adjusting the request interval, we found that the total energy savings resulting from our proposal exceeded its threshold value of 50%. Our final dataset, which contains the data collected in our experiment, has been made available for further research. To optimize the selection of WiFi equipment for each location, we suggest a new two-layer strategy. The first layer consists of all the possible locations that report channel information, while the second layer comprises nodes in each location that are selected based on the topology of the provider's network to minimize the load on the provider's management system. To determine which location should report its channel information, we use the level of interest concept, which relies on the topology of the provider's network to minimize the load on the provider's management system. By testing the level of interest concept in our experiment, we found that the locations of interest and their interest values exceeded their threshold values of 80% and 77%, respectively.
